quote.text: words in the question do not count as application

takeaways: Use a different detail from the scenario for each point. Reusing the same one, or copying words from the question, earns nothing extra.
Do not give a mirror answer. If you say one thing is out of date, saying the other is up to date gains no further mark.
Analysis means explaining how or why. Do not jump straight to profit and do not add new points of knowledge.
In part (e) and the (b) questions, give a decision with a reason and say why the alternative was rejected.
Be precise on definitions and units. Say a single individual for sole trader, and give % in margin answers.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Standards were high overall, and most candidates knew the subject well.
Most chose suitable sources of finance, such as retained profit or bank loans.
Most knew primary and secondary market research, and many gained all the knowledge and analysis marks.
Candidates knew sustainable development and production methods well, and many scored full marks on the first.
mistakes: Definitions were imprecise, for example repeating the word sole or saying working capital is the day to day costs.
Many reused the same application or analysis for both points, or copied words from the question.
Common wrong answers confused motivators with hygiene factors, and price skimming with penetration pricing.
Many assumed a niche market or a multinational always means higher profit.
Many gave only a summary in part (e), or left out a decision.
fix: Make each definition precise. Say a single individual for sole trader.
Use a different piece of scenario information for each point.
Explain how or why a point matters. Do not restate it or add new points.
Do not mirror one point to cover both sides of a comparison.
Finish part (e) with a decision, a reason, and a comparison with the alternative.

questions.issue: Typical wrong answers gave hygiene factors, and others listed levels from a needs theory.
questions.fix: Name true motivators such as recognition or achievement.

questions.issue: Answers lacked precision, such as saying higher span of control and vaguely saying communication is easier.
questions.fix: Say wide span of control and a short chain of command, and mention the speed of communication.

questions.issue: A common misconception was that a niche market means more revenue or profit, and some reused one application point.
questions.fix: Stick to less competition and the chance of higher prices, with different context for each.

questions.topic: Sources of finance for a partnership
questions.issue: A common mistake was a short-term source such as an overdraft. Some gave share sales, which a partnership cannot use, and others gave disadvantages.
questions.fix: Pick a source that suits the business type and explain an advantage of it.

questions.issue: Most summarised earlier points. Some wrote about the role of research, or gave mirror answers.
questions.fix: Weigh advantages and disadvantages of each type and finish with a supported decision.

questions.issue: Candidates confused skimming with penetration and wrote about issues with new products.
questions.fix: Compare skimming with other pricing methods and decide whether it is best.

questions.issue: A common mistake was leaving out the times 100 or the percentage sign. Others gave dollars.
questions.fix: Use the profit margin formula, multiply by 100 and write the % sign.

questions.issue: Some confused minimum wage with ethical issues, or thought paying above it means paying less.
questions.fix: Treat it as a legal control and balance higher costs against motivated staff.

papers.title: Case study
well: Many candidates were well prepared and most finished the paper.
Many knew why a new business is at greater risk of failure.
Many compared two locations and calculated total costs.
Most could outline an advantage and a disadvantage of holding inventory, and most knew that higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing.
mistakes: Some candidates had knowledge but only made simple statements, mostly in the (b) questions.
Weaker answers repeated the reason as the explanation.
Candidates listed advantages and disadvantages without explaining the effects, or gave a mirror point for the other business type.
Some explained the wrong management function, or gave the role of a manager.
Weaker conclusions repeated earlier points, and some used cash and profit as if they were the same.
fix: Explain the consequence of every advantage and disadvantage for the business in the case.
Never write the mirror of a point to fill the other side.
Say which cost is higher. Do not write vague words like higher costs.
Compare the options directly and use the data given to calculate. Words like high, low, cheap or expensive are not a comparison.
In a recommendation, justify your choice and say why you rejected the alternatives.

questions.issue: Weaker answers repeated the reason as the explanation.
questions.fix: Name the reason, then explain the effect, such as poor planning from lack of experience.

questions.issue: Points were listed, generic, or mirrored, which kept answers out of the higher levels.
questions.fix: Explain the effect of each advantage and disadvantage and justify your choice and rejection.

questions.issue: Explanations did not match the function named, or described a manager's role.
questions.fix: Learn each function and give an explanation that matches it.

questions.issue: Weaker answers just repeated the appendix and used words like cheap or expensive. Profit could not be judged without a price.
questions.fix: Calculate total and unit costs, and consider the effect of power cuts on output.

questions.issue: Some listed an advantage and disadvantage with no link to the business, or just said higher cost.
questions.fix: Say which cost rises, and link the benefit to the business, such as meeting a sudden demand.

questions.issue: Discussion lacked detail and conclusions repeated earlier points.
questions.fix: Develop one or two points for each channel and justify your final choice.

questions.issue: Application was repeated, the loan amount was often missing, and some treated profit as a cash inflow.
questions.fix: Use different case details for each item and include the amount where one is given.

questions.issue: Weaker answers stayed with basic statements and did not explain what it means for the business.
questions.fix: Link each change to the business, such as higher disposable income raising demand.

quote.text: Without analysis, it is not possible to access evaluation

takeaways: Be precise in definitions. Name both key parts, such as ownership and government, or GDP and time.
Give a different piece of context for each point. Using the same one twice, or words already in the question, earns no extra mark.
Develop each point differently to earn analysis. Restating the point or adding a new point of knowledge does not count.
Read what the question asks. A few answers explained why a problem happened when asked how to overcome it, and some gave profit methods for a cash flow question.
Evaluation needs a decision plus a reason, such as why one option beats the alternative. A summary of earlier points does not count.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Many answers showed good knowledge of the subject.
Most knew the advantages and disadvantages of primary market research and ways to fix a cash flow problem.
Many identified four stages of recruitment and a benefit of a motivated workforce.
Candidates who understood on-the-job training explained both an advantage and a disadvantage of it.
mistakes: Some definitions described features instead of defining the term, such as limited liability for a private limited company.
Many did not mention that sustainable development protects the environment for future generations.
Some did not link points to the context, and many reused the same application for both points.
Some wrote about profit, or the cause of a cash flow problem, instead of ways to overcome it, and confused payables with receivables.
Candidates confused on-the-job training with induction, listed recruitment activities instead of stages, and counted training as a recruitment stage.
Evaluation was rare and usually a summary of earlier points.
fix: Define the term, not its features. A private limited company sells shares to friends and family.
Define public sector as owned by the government, not just run by it.
Show the effect of a method on cash inflows or cash outflows, not just that it is useful.
Name actual stages of recruitment, such as job description or interview, not a description of the task.
Name a specific communication method, such as email, and say why it helps.

questions.issue: Candidates described limited liability, mixed it with the private sector, or wrote about customers instead of shareholders.
questions.fix: Say it sells shares, and only to friends and family.

questions.issue: Many left out who is being protected, or described how a business can be sustainable.
questions.fix: Define it as protecting the environment so future generations can meet their needs.

questions.issue: Many gave advantages of a method. Some gave profit methods, and a few explained why the problem happened.
questions.fix: Pick a method such as a loan or delayed supplier payments and explain how it raises inflows or lowers outflows.

questions.issue: Candidates named one point and added new knowledge instead of analysis. Evaluation was rare.
questions.fix: Develop each point, compare channels and decide with a reason.

questions.issue: Some repeated the same idea twice, such as productivity and efficiency, or wrote vaguely about working harder.
questions.fix: Give two distinct benefits, such as output and quality.

questions.issue: Some described activities or thought training is a stage. A few gave person specification and job specification as two stages.
questions.fix: Name actual stages, such as job description, person specification, advertising the vacancy and interviewing.

questions.issue: Words like easier or effective had no reason. Some named visual or face to face without a method.
questions.fix: Name the method, explain why it helps, such as a written record, and compare it with others.

questions.issue: Many divided the figures and got 1.3 instead of subtracting break-even output.
questions.fix: Subtract break-even output from current output and show working.

papers.title: Case study
well: Many candidates showed good knowledge across the syllabus topics that were tested.
Many applied their answers to the café business in the case study.
Most explained why some businesses stay small, such as the preference of the owner.
Most gave clear advantages and disadvantages of cost-plus pricing, and most knew what short-term and long-term finance are used for.
mistakes: Some had little understanding of internal and external growth, cost-plus pricing and the effects of higher interest rates.
Some stated a reason, or listed advantages and disadvantages, without explaining the effect on the business.
Some reversed quality control and quality assurance, or swapped the uses of short-term and long-term finance.
Most conclusions on the promotion question repeated earlier points.
Most did not include wage calculations, or did one for a single job applicant only.
fix: Check the marks for each question so you know how much explanation is needed.
Answer from the point of view of the business, not its employees.
Develop a few points fully. A long list of simple statements is less effective.
In a recommendation, justify your choice, apply it to the case and say why the other option was rejected.
Think about short term and long term effects to reach the higher levels in a conclusion.

questions.issue: Some only stated the reason. Some wrongly gave reducing competition or avoiding a takeover.
questions.fix: State the reason, then explain why it keeps the business small, such as too little finance to grow.

questions.issue: Some listed points or gave definitions only. Some reversed the two, such as placing inspectors under quality assurance.
questions.fix: Explain how each method affects the café, then recommend one and say why the other is weaker.

questions.issue: Some thought the business should simply charge more to make more profit, or missed that the benefit is profit on each item.
questions.fix: Give an advantage and a disadvantage and link each one to the café.

questions.issue: Several wrote how to achieve each aim, not why it suits the business. Most conclusions were repetition.
questions.fix: Argue why each aim fits this business and support your choice with a reason you have not already used.

questions.issue: Some swapped the reasons for the two types. A few gave sources that do not suit the size and ownership of the business.
questions.fix: Link short-term finance to day to day expenses and long-term finance to expansion or non-current assets.

questions.topic: New café or taking over a competitor
questions.issue: Some were vague, such as saying a takeover is expensive with no reason. Some treated the takeover as a partnership or franchise.
questions.fix: Give the reason behind each claim and avoid points that fit both options.

questions.issue: Many linked the rise straight to raw material costs, lower disposable income or lower profit with no explanation. Some thought it means inflation or government revenue.
questions.fix: Explain the link through saving and borrowing, such as a higher cost of loans for expansion.

questions.issue: Most made only simple comparisons from the Insert. Most left out wage calculations or did one applicant only.
questions.fix: Compare all three applicants in context and support the comparison with calculations.

quote.text: summary of earlier points is not evaluation

takeaways: Write precise definitions. Use the exact idea, such as owned not run for ownership, and total costs not just costs for profit.
For application, pick a different detail from the scenario for each point. Reusing the same detail only earns one mark.
Analysis means explaining how or why a point matters. Repeating the point, or adding a new point, earns nothing extra.
Part (e) needs a decision, a reason, and why the other option is weaker. Repeating what you already wrote earns no evaluation marks.
On the case study papers, a few developed points beat a long list. Listed points stay at Level 1.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Most knew the support governments give new businesses, such as grants and lower tax.
Many saw that an economic boom raises sales and some saw the risk of rising costs.
Most could name two methods of external growth.
Most could state two different pricing methods.
mistakes: Some found it hard to show a clear understanding of terms such as profit, cash flow, added value, economic boom and sustainable development.
Some reused the same application point, or made no reference to the business, and so missed application marks.
Candidates gave decisions in part (e) without a clear reason, or just summarised earlier points.
A noticeable number thought price skimming means a low price, and lean production was confused with flow production or its features.
Market research answers named only primary and secondary, not specific methods.
Diseconomies of scale and retained profit were poorly understood, and some candidates left them blank.
fix: Learn precise definitions. A partnership is owned by two or more people, so say owned.
In list type questions only the first two answers count, so put your best two first.
Use a distinctly different piece of application and analysis for each point of knowledge.
Name specific methods of market research, such as a survey, not just primary or secondary.
End part (e) with a decision supported by a reason and a comparison with the alternative.

questions.issue: Some described a merger and scored zero. Many lost a mark by saying run or manage instead of own.
questions.fix: Say two or more people own an unincorporated business.

questions.topic: Pricing methods for a new business
questions.issue: Many could not explain their chosen methods. Some thought skimming means a low price.
questions.fix: Name each method, explain it and finish with a decision linked to winning customers.

questions.issue: Some confused it with flow production or listed features instead of advantages.
questions.fix: State an advantage, such as less waste or less stock, then explain the impact on the business.

questions.issue: Many gave only primary and secondary. Few went beyond cost or time of each method.
questions.fix: Name two specific methods, explain how each helps decisions and justify the better one.

questions.issue: Many said it calculates profit, confusing it with an income statement.
questions.fix: Say it helps planning and supports loan applications by showing expected cash in and out.

questions.issue: Many confused it with multinational businesses and listed benefits of operating abroad.
questions.fix: Give reasons, such as free trade agreements or better transport and communication links.

questions.issue: Weaker answers tried to reuse economies of scale, and a noticeable share did not attempt it.
questions.fix: Learn one diseconomy and explain how larger size raises average costs.

questions.issue: Weaker answers confused profit with cash flow. Others discussed loans instead.
questions.fix: Say it avoids repayment but may delay expansion, and judge if it is enough.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Most candidates showed good subject knowledge and attempted every question.
Most understood profit as revenue minus costs and gave good examples of expenses.
Most gave correct reasons why new businesses are at greater risk of failure, and many explained two named methods of communication.
Strong answers compared methods of motivation to reach a judgement.
mistakes: Definitions lacked precision, such as costs instead of total costs, or repeating the word batch.
Many reused the same application and analysis for both points.
Some repeated the knowledge point instead of explaining how or why, or added new points.
Candidates confused quality assurance with quality control, market segmentation with market research, and job rotation with job enrichment.
Most of those who attempted evaluation gave no reason to back up the decision.
fix: Make definitions precise. Your wording does not need to match the coursebook if the meaning is clear.
Use information from the stem for each point, with a different detail each time.
Explain how or why your point matters. Do not restate it.
Do not define terms the question does not ask you to define.
Use a decision and a supporting reason in part (e). Do not bring in new points.

questions.issue: Many missed that items move through production together as a group. Some described flow production.
questions.fix: Say goods are made in groups that move together through each stage. Do not repeat the word batch.

questions.issue: Some described inspectors checking at the end, which is quality control.
questions.fix: Focus on preventing faults throughout production, and use the product from the stem.

questions.issue: Many wrote about market research or mass versus niche marketing.
questions.fix: Explain how splitting the market lets the business design for one group and target its marketing.

questions.issue: Many included expenses such as rent and salaries, which do not affect gross profit.
questions.fix: Focus on lower sales and higher cost of sales, and use the table.

questions.issue: Some wrote about production in a retailer, and some about disadvantages of external recruitment.
questions.fix: Give advantages of promoting from within and keep the retail setting in mind.

questions.issue: Many just said it would motivate staff. Some thought job rotation gives rest breaks, or named only financial and non financial.
questions.fix: Name each method and explain how it raises motivation, then compare them for a decision.

questions.issue: Answers talked about control or running the business, or listed sole traders and companies.
questions.fix: Define it by ownership: businesses owned by private individuals or groups.

questions.issue: Some gave two types of pollution, which counts once. Others wrongly assumed the business made cars.
questions.fix: Give two different external costs and tie each to the actual product.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Most could name a role of packaging, such as information, attracting customers or protection.
Candidates who knew the product life cycle scored highly.
Many gained the marks for a reason a business might stay small, such as owner preference or demand.
Most showed good knowledge of sole trader advantages and disadvantages.
mistakes: Application remained weak across the paper and was often missing from part (c) and (d) answers.
Many reused the same application and analysis for both points.
Many confused ethical issues with legal ones, such as the minimum wage.
Many named advertising or pricing when asked about sales promotion.
Many wrote financial reasons for staying small when the question excluded them.
Most evaluation was a decision with no reason, or a repeat of the earlier points.
fix: Use the scenario details in every part (c) and (d) answer, with a different reference for each point.
Analyse for the stakeholder named in the question, not for the business in general.
Learn the difference between ethical choices and legal duties.
Read what type of promotion or method is asked for, and answer only that.
Explain how a method works, such as how free samples encourage sales.

questions.issue: Many confused ethical and legal issues. Analysis was about the business, not the named stakeholder.
questions.fix: Use fair pay or paying suppliers on time and explain the effect on the stakeholder named.

questions.issue: Many wrote about advertising or pricing. Weaker responses could not develop points.
questions.fix: Name methods such as free samples or buy one get one free and explain how they lift sales.

questions.issue: Candidates gave vague answers such as capital, or thought profit measures size.
questions.fix: Use number of employees or sales, not profit.

questions.issue: Many gave financial reasons the question excluded, and few used the context.
questions.fix: Use owner choice or low demand and link each to the type and product of the business.

questions.topic: Cash flow problems from slow payers
questions.issue: Some described the table. Others were vague or mixed up cash flow with profit.
questions.fix: Say late customer payments cut cash inflows, and use the table data to show it.

questions.issue: Most gave benefits to the business or just examples, not gains to third parties.
questions.fix: Define them as gains to people outside the business, and give an example.

questions.issue: A common mistake was assuming wages are a motivator.
questions.fix: Treat wages as a hygiene factor and opportunities for promotion as a motivator.

questions.issue: Many drifted into motivation or tiredness, or wrote about part-time staff. Analysis was missing.
questions.fix: Focus on full-time staff only and explain each benefit before judging.

papers.title: Case study
well: Candidates were generally well prepared and most finished the paper.
Many had sound knowledge of moving from sole trader to private limited company.
Mass market advantages and disadvantages, and bank loan points, were well answered.
Those who applied answers to the case scored higher.
mistakes: The weakest understanding was of factors influencing location and of financial analysis.
Some did not apply their knowledge to the case. On question 1(a) application carried half the marks.
Piece-rate was less well understood than bonuses and job rotation.
Very few answers developed promotion points into chains of reasoning. Conclusions repeated earlier points.
Financial analysis showed weak numeracy, some missed that figures were in thousands, and some treated a forecast as past data.
fix: Ask who owns the business, its size, and whether it makes things or sells services before writing.
Explain each point as a chain so it reaches Level 2. Lists stay at Level 1.
Finish with a justified decision, applied to the case, that says why the other options were rejected.
Calculate and label liquidity ratios such as current and acid test, then use them for the decision.
Learn government influences on location, such as grants and job schemes.

questions.issue: Some did not apply their knowledge to the case, and application carried half the marks.
questions.fix: State an advantage and a disadvantage and show what each means for the owner in the case.

questions.issue: Simple statements earned Level 1. Piece-rate was less well understood.
questions.fix: Chain each method to its effect and finish with a justified recommendation.

questions.issue: Knowledge of government influences was generally weak. Only the best conclusions avoided repeating earlier points.
questions.fix: Explain each factor's impact in context and say which is most significant.

questions.issue: Very few built a reasoned chain, and few conclusions were well justified.
questions.fix: Weigh benefits against costs for each method, then justify your choice.

questions.issue: The effect of business profit tax was less well answered than income tax.
questions.fix: Link higher profit tax to lower retained profit and then to less investment.

questions.issue: Weak numeracy, missed that figures were in thousands, and some treated a forecast as history.
questions.fix: Calculate and label ratios, note the units and years, and justify your advice.

papers.title: Case study
well: Candidates were generally well prepared and most completed the paper.
Most gave stakeholder objectives clearly, such as dividends, prompt payment and better pay.
Many recognised that a recession cuts spending and reduces sales.
Stronger answers used gross profit and margin calculations to justify a takeover choice.
mistakes: The weakest understanding was of problems entering a new country, absenteeism and labour turnover, and recessions.
Some thought the business made goods in the new country when it only sold there.
Some wrote drawbacks when asked for benefits, or how to reduce absenteeism.
A significant number wrongly thought inflation rises in a recession.
Calculation errors were common. Some confused gross profit with profit, and several weaker answers left out the dollar sign or the word million.
fix: Answer from the stakeholder's point of view, not the business's.
Apply the objective to the case, using details such as the number of countries.
Develop each point so it reaches Level 2. Explain why a benefit helps the business.
When comparing options, be consistent. Do not say transport is dearer for one and cheaper for the other.
Label every calculated figure and link it to the decision.

questions.issue: Cultural differences were named but few explained the effect on demand. Some wrote about production abroad.
questions.fix: Explain how the problem affects sales or marketing in the new country.

questions.topic: Benefits of low absenteeism and turnover
questions.issue: Benefits were not developed. Some listed drawbacks or ways to reduce the problems.
questions.fix: Explain why each benefit helps the business and keep to benefits only.

questions.issue: Weaker answers described the stakeholder's role or the business's view.
questions.fix: State what each group wants, and apply it to the case.

questions.issue: Most stayed at simple statements. Recommendations lacked reasons.
questions.fix: Explain both a gain and a cost of each way, then compare them for the business.

questions.issue: Some flipped points, and weaker answers were vague, such as cheaper. Several cited tariffs the case did not mention.
questions.fix: Be consistent, justify claims on cost and quality, and recommend with reasons.

questions.issue: A significant number thought inflation rises in a recession.
questions.fix: Link recession to lower spending, falling sales and a larger pool of labour.

questions.issue: Weaker answers gave calculations only, or loose comparisons. Some mixed up gross profit and profit.
questions.fix: Calculate and label margins, then explain how the figures help the business.

papers.title: Case study
well: Candidates were generally quite well prepared and most finished.
Many gave two advantages and two disadvantages of buying a franchise.
Most gave at least one benefit of market segmentation and applied it to the business.
Many identified four external sources of finance.
mistakes: The weakest understanding was of profitability and liquidity ratios.
Weaker answers wrote about starting a business, not buying a franchise.
Many stated facts about candidates for a job without explaining why they are an advantage or a disadvantage.
Location answers were lists of advantages and disadvantages. Level 1 was common.
Some thought job enrichment meant promotion, and many answers were generic.
fix: Apply each answer to the business in the case.
Explain why a stated fact is an advantage or a disadvantage, for example how a long training period delays revenue.
Develop fewer points well. Do not comment on every item in the data.
Justify the recommendation without repeating earlier points, and say why the others are less suitable.
Learn the difference between profit and profitability, and what liquidity ratios show.

questions.issue: Weaker answers described starting a business generally. Many were not applied to the case.
questions.fix: Cover franchise points such as brand, training, licence fee and shared profit, and apply them.

questions.issue: Points were stated with no reasons. Some wrongly assumed one candidate had already been trained.
questions.fix: Say why each fact helps or hurts, and justify the pick without repeating.

questions.issue: Answers were simple lists of data, stuck at Level 1.
questions.fix: Develop two or three points on each location and justify your choice over the others.

questions.issue: Weaker answers described what the money would be used for, not the source.
questions.fix: Name each source and explain how it works.

questions.issue: The lowest scoring question. Candidates mixed up profit and profitability, and could not develop liquidity.
questions.fix: Define each ratio, say what it shows and why a business cares.

questions.issue: Candidates identified effects but did not explain in enough detail why each one affects the business.
questions.fix: Use the data given, name the effect, and explain how it changes sales, costs or competition.

questions.issue: Some assumed job enrichment means promotion. Many answers were generic.
questions.fix: Say enrichment gives extra, harder tasks, which may need training, and apply it to the case.

quote.text: A good understanding of double entry bookkeeping is essential

takeaways: Dates and correct labels were missed again and again in journals, ledger accounts and club accounts. Put both in every time.
For five mark advice questions, plan first, give points for and against, then finish with a clear recommendation.
Show workings for ratios and give the right unit, such as a percentage sign or days, and two decimal places.
Do not add extra items to an account. Many ledger and control accounts lost marks for items that did not belong.
Read each question slowly, in multiple choice too. The report asks for every item to be read with great care before an option is chosen.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many candidates had a good understanding of the topics and picked the right option on many items.
Most candidates answered correctly on the accountant's tasks, the purpose of a trial balance, and which balances sit on its credit side.
The disadvantage of sole trader ownership was well known.
mistakes: Some candidates put the opening entry in a suspense account on the wrong side.
Some candidates counted depreciation on a van that had been sold.
Some thought amounts owed to the business belong in the capital and liabilities section.
Some thought a partner's capital account changes with profit and drawings.
Some thought sales income is only recognised when a cheque arrives.
fix: Check which side of the suspense account the opening entry belongs on.
Leave out assets that have already been sold when you total accumulated depreciation.
Remember that capital and liabilities show what the owner and others have provided, not what is owed to the business.
When a partner has both a capital account and a current account, profit share and drawings go through the current account, so the capital account does not move.
Recognise income when goods are sold, not when payment arrives.

questions.issue: Most knew the amount but some put the opening entry on the debit side.
questions.fix: Work out which side balances the trial balance before placing the entry.

questions.issue: Some candidates found it hard to calculate the balance and decide if it was a debit or credit.
questions.fix: Add and subtract in order and check the sign of the result to decide the side.

questions.issue: Some candidates included depreciation for a van that had been sold.
questions.fix: Only calculate depreciation on vehicles still held, and use the correct months for a part year.

questions.topic: Change in provision for doubtful debts
questions.issue: Some found it hard to work out the change in the provision from one year to the next.
questions.fix: Calculate each year's provision, then charge only the increase to the income statement.

questions.issue: Some thought amounts owed to the business belong here.
questions.fix: Remember that capital and liabilities show where the resources came from.

questions.issue: Some thought the capital account moves with profit and drawings.
questions.fix: Where a partner has a current account, put the profit share and drawings there, not in the capital account.

questions.issue: Some thought income is not recognised until a cheque arrives.
questions.fix: Recognise income when the goods are sold, not when cash is received.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Candidates made a good attempt at the income statement and many earned high marks.
Correcting journal entries was a familiar topic and many answers earned good marks.
Many candidates were familiar with ratio calculations and gained good marks.
Many advice answers earned three or four marks, with sensible points for and against.
mistakes: Dates were left out of journals and ledger accounts, and totals were labelled wrongly.
Purchases accounts included the wrong totals, left out cash purchases or included returns.
Control accounts omitted the opening balance and included items that did not belong.
Income statement labels were missing, and rental income was added to sales or deducted from expenses.
Candidates did not show workings for ratios, and left out percentage signs, days or two decimal places.
Many answers on refurbishing a rented shop missed that the premises were rented, and did not explain why expenses might rise.
fix: Put a date and a correct label on every journal and ledger entry.
Use the total of the purchases journal in the purchases account and include cash purchases but not returns.
Start a control account with the opening balance and leave out unrelated items.
Label the cost of sales, the gross profit and the profit for the year, and add rental income to gross profit as other income.
Show workings for each ratio and finish with the unit and two decimal places.

questions.issue: Candidates used the wrong totals, listed purchases one by one, missed cash purchases or included returns.
questions.fix: Post the total of the purchases journal, add cash purchases and leave out returns.

questions.issue: The opening balance was missing, extra items were included and individual purchases were listed instead of totals.
questions.fix: Start with the opening balance and use only totals from the books.

questions.issue: The bank overdraft was not adjusted for bank charges, and accrued expenses and prepaid rental income were often omitted or mislabelled.
questions.fix: Adjust the overdraft for charges and show each accrued and prepaid item with its own label.

questions.issue: Candidates focused on sales and financing and missed that the shop was rented, and gave no reason for higher expenses.
questions.fix: Look for who owns the premises, give reasons for each point and consider the risk of spending on rented property.

questions.issue: Candidates adjusted for all the errors, and many left out the original total.
questions.fix: Start with the original total and adjust only for the errors that affect the trial balance.

questions.issue: Many focused on liquidity and thought receivables are not part of sales.
questions.fix: Link it to irrecoverable debts, provision changes and the effect of paying suppliers later.

questions.issue: Subscriptions and expenses prepaid and accrued were classified wrongly, and year end figures were used.
questions.fix: Classify each prepaid and accrued item correctly and use opening figures only.

questions.issue: Candidates did not calculate purchases, or used the total paid without adjusting for opening and closing balances.
questions.fix: Adjust payments for opening and closing balances to find purchases, and avoid abbreviations.

quote.text: A thorough understanding of basic principles is essential.

takeaways: In written questions, use the facts in the scenario. The report calls general lines such as costs will increase too vague.
Ledger accounts go wrong when double entry is shaky, so practise the basic entries until they are automatic.
Do not put irrelevant items in an account or statement. Many candidates added things that did not belong.
Follow instructions such as two decimal places, a percentage sign, or the :1 in a ratio.
End every advice question with a clear recommendation.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Candidates did well on twenty questions, including 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9 and 14.
Questions 19, 21 to 25, 27, 29 to 32, 34 and 35 were also answered well.
mistakes: Candidates were weaker where the wording or style of a question was less familiar to them.
Wrong options were common on the trial balance and the bank reconciliation statement. The report stresses that neither is part of the double entry system.
Wrong options were common on how treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure affects profit and non-current assets.
Wrong options were common on how errors in valuing work in progress and finished goods change cost of sales.
A wrong option was common on the sales ledger control account, which shows total credit sales and no cash sales.
fix: Remember that a trial balance and a bank reconciliation check the books and are not part of double entry.
Keep the discount received account in the general ledger, and only credit supplier accounts in the purchases ledger.
If capital expenditure is treated as revenue expenditure, expenses are overstated, profit is understated and non-current assets are understated.
Remember that the work in progress valuation changes both cost of production and cost of sales, but the finished goods valuation changes cost of sales only.
Use total credit sales only in a sales ledger control account.

questions.issue: One wrong option was a common choice. The discount received account sits in the general ledger, not the purchases ledger.
questions.fix: Only credit supplier accounts belong in the purchases ledger.

questions.issue: One wrong option was a common choice. The report points to which inventory figure a trial balance holds and to its place outside double entry.
questions.fix: A trial balance is a list of ledger balances. It includes opening inventory but not closing inventory.

questions.issue: Two wrong options were common. Once the cash book is updated, bank charges no longer cause a difference.
questions.fix: Bank charges appear in both records after updating. Deduct an unpresented cheque from the bank statement balance.

questions.issue: Two wrong options were common on the effect on profit and on non-current assets.
questions.fix: Expenses are overstated, profit is understated and non-current assets are understated.

questions.issue: One wrong option was a common choice. The year 2 charge is worked on the value left after the year 1 depreciation.
questions.fix: Apply the percentage to cost less depreciation to date. Debit the income statement and credit the provision for depreciation account.

questions.issue: Two wrong options were common on how each valuation error changes cost of production and cost of sales.
questions.fix: Understated work in progress overstates cost of production and cost of sales. Overstated finished goods understate cost of sales.

questions.issue: One wrong option was a common choice. A higher selling price does not make goods sell faster.
questions.fix: Lower inventory means faster turnover, but a price rise does not.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Some candidates linked their knowledge to the scenario and gave good arguments for and against.
Many candidates showed good understanding of double entry and the preparation of financial statements.
Most understood how to keep a three column cash book. Good answers had dated entries, suitable details and balances brought down.
Good answers on the capital account showed that profit increases capital and drawings reduce it.
mistakes: Written answers were general and not tied to the scenario.
Ledger accounts included irrelevant items, were reversed, or used the wrong totals.
Disposal accounts, depreciation accounts and asset accounts were mixed up, with items put in the wrong account.
Capital and revenue items were confused, particularly delivery cost and insurance.
Candidates confused realisation with historic cost, and prudence with money measurement.
Abbreviations were used in labels, and percentage and ratio answers lacked the correct format.
fix: Use the figures and facts in the scenario in every written answer and finish with a clear recommendation.
Keep each account to its own entries and balance it when asked.
In disposals, move the cost to disposal from the asset account and the depreciation to date from the provision account.
Learn capital and revenue expenditure properly, including delivery cost and insurance.
Learn the accounting principles and name the right one.

questions.issue: Many did not transfer the monthly total from the cash book and some entered individual amounts or reversed the account.
questions.fix: Credit the monthly total from the cash book and balance the account.

questions.issue: Many gave generic points and missed that the trader sold very little on credit.
questions.fix: Link each point to the situation described, such as how few credit sales there were.

questions.issue: Candidates only said everything is entered twice and missed that control accounts are checking devices outside double entry.
questions.fix: Define duality fully and say that control accounts sit outside the double entry system, so duality does not apply to them.

questions.issue: Items that do not belong, such as the depreciation provision and the sale proceeds, were often included.
questions.fix: Show the opening balance, transfer the cost of the sold vehicle to disposal, then balance the account.

questions.issue: Candidates did not use the life expectancy of the old fittings or the recent large spend on a new vehicle, and many missed that depreciation would be higher.
questions.fix: Use every piece of information given, discuss higher depreciation and end with a recommendation.

questions.issue: Candidates used gross sales instead of net sales for the denominator, and left out the percentage sign and two decimal places.
questions.fix: Use net sales, show two decimal places and add the percentage sign.

questions.issue: Candidates started from the original bank balance and deducted the unpresented cheque.
questions.fix: Start from the corrected bank balance and add the unpresented cheque.

questions.issue: Many deducted inventory from the receivables total instead of from total current assets, left out the two decimal places or omitted the :1.
questions.fix: Deduct inventory from total current assets, show two decimal places and write the ratio as :1.

quote.text: Too many answers were produced on a standardised basis

takeaways: Write every label in full. Balance b/d and profit for the year are right. Abbreviations lose marks.
Advice questions need the scenario's facts, a reason for each point and a clear recommendation, not one standard answer.
Most mark losses came from basic double entry. Start each account with its opening balance and keep irrelevant items out.
Practise the calculation questions in multiple choice, because the report says some candidates found them hard.
Follow instructions in ratio answers, such as two decimal places and a percentage sign.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many candidates understood the topics and picked the right option on many items.
Most candidates answered correctly on the bookkeeper's tasks, the book of prime entry for credit purchases, and the items on a statement of financial position.
Most knew why a sole trader might gain from forming a partnership.
mistakes: Some candidates found the calculation questions hard.
Bulk buying discounts were wrongly treated as discounts that appear in ledger accounts.
On the bank reconciliation question, some stopped at the original cash book balance and others added the unpresented cheque and deducted the bank charges.
Some thought goods returned to suppliers come from the general journal.
In incomplete records questions, some candidates subtracted figures that should have been added.
Some thought partners' salaries are an expense in the income statement.
fix: Practise the calculation questions, because the report says some candidates found them hard.
Remember that a discount for bulk buying is never entered in the ledger accounts.
To get from the bank statement balance to the updated cash book balance, deduct unpresented cheques. Bank charges are already in the updated cash book.
Use the right book for each item. Returns to suppliers come from the purchases returns journal, not the general journal.
Check whether each figure in an incomplete records calculation should be added or subtracted.

questions.topic: Types of discount in ledger accounts
questions.issue: Some thought a supplier gave a discount for buying in bulk, when the ledger entry showed a discount for paying early.
questions.fix: Read what the ledger account shows. Only discounts for paying early are recorded in ledger accounts.

questions.topic: Journal to correct a wrongly debited account
questions.issue: Candidates found the correcting entry hard because the account needed double the wrong amount credited.
questions.fix: Cancel the wrong debit and then make the correct entry, so the credit equals twice the error.

questions.issue: Some gave the cash book balance before the bank charges. Others added the unpresented cheque and took off the bank charges.
questions.fix: Deduct the unpresented cheque from the bank statement balance. Leave the bank charges alone, because the updated cash book already includes them.

questions.issue: A significant number thought returns to suppliers are recorded in the general journal.
questions.fix: Learn which book of prime entry each item in the control account comes from.

questions.issue: Some gave the opening balance on the provision, not the closing one.
questions.fix: Find the provision at the end of the year, including that year's charge.

questions.topic: Change in provision for doubtful debts
questions.issue: Candidates found the change but thought it was a debit to the provision.
questions.fix: An increase in the provision is a credit to the provision account.

questions.issue: Some treated a partner's salary as an income statement expense.
questions.fix: Show salaries in the appropriation account as a share of profit.

questions.issue: Some took off the cash payments and the drawings when they should have added them.
questions.fix: Add the cash payments, drawings, banked cash and cash in hand to find the sales total.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many candidates understood the topics examined and chose the right option on many items.
Most found the question on how owner's equity is calculated straightforward.
Most found the profit from changes in capital question straightforward.
mistakes: Some candidates found the calculation questions challenging.
Some miscalculated the petty cash restoration, and some subtracted figures in a suspense account correction instead of adding.
Some used the wrong bank reconciliation steps with unpresented cheques and uncredited deposits.
Some calculated depreciation for one year only, or left out the residual value.
Some did not deduct the written off debt before calculating the provision for doubtful debts.
Some thought an increase in work in progress would increase cost of production and cost of sales.
fix: Practise multiple choice calculations regularly.
Work out the cash needed to restore the petty cash imprest from the amount spent less any refund received.
When an account was credited with one amount instead of being debited with another, add the two amounts to find the correction.
Use the cost less residual value, and multiply by the number of years.
Deduct the irrecoverable debt first, then calculate the provision.

questions.issue: Some used the opening imprest in the wrong way and got a figure that was too high.
questions.fix: Take the amount spent, less any refund received, and restore the imprest by that amount.

questions.issue: Some subtracted the two amounts when one account had been credited instead of debited, so the entry was too small.
questions.fix: When an item was posted to the wrong side, correct both the wrong credit and the missing debit.

questions.issue: Some calculated one year only, and others left out residual value.
questions.fix: Subtract the residual value, divide by the life and multiply by the years elapsed.

questions.issue: Some found it hard to adjust the rent due for the year for rent paid in advance at the start and at the end.
questions.fix: Start with the rent due for the year, add the rent received in advance at the end of the year and take away the rent received in advance at the start.

questions.issue: Some did not deduct the amount written off before calculating the provision.
questions.fix: Write off the irrecoverable debt first, then work out the provision.

questions.issue: Some used one partner's share of residual profit instead of the whole residual profit.
questions.fix: Find total residual profit first, then work out the salary.

questions.issue: Some thought cost of production and cost of sales would increase.
questions.fix: An increase in work in progress reduces cost of production and cost of sales.

questions.issue: Some did not know that information has to be timely to be relevant.
questions.fix: Learn what makes information relevant, including timing.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Most candidates earned over half the marks on the petty cash book.
Many answers to the farm shop and other advice questions listed advantages and disadvantages and gave a recommendation.
There were many good responses to correcting errors, with high marks for some candidates.
Many candidates were well prepared for the manufacturing account and earned high marks.
mistakes: Candidates used unacceptable abbreviations in accounts and statements, and wrote vague wording instead of the account name.
Many did not know how to prepare an opening journal entry.
Ledger accounts left out the opening balance, included extraneous items or were completely reversed.
Candidates put revenue items like insurance and petrol into capital expenditure.
The suspense account and bank correction answers left out opening figures and included items that did not belong.
Many struggled to define equity or work out return on capital employed with the right figures.
fix: Write full labels such as Balance b/d and profit for the year, and never use abbreviations such as NP or MV.
Learn the opening journal entry as one entry for assets, liabilities and capital.
Start every account with the opening balance, use the account name as the detail and leave out extra items.
Check capital and revenue expenditure carefully, and keep running costs out of capital.
In suspense and bank questions, start with the figure before the corrections and include only items that affect them.

questions.issue: Many tried separate entries for each asset or just subtracted liabilities from assets.
questions.fix: Write one journal with each asset and liability as an entry and capital to balance.

questions.issue: Candidates understood the entries but used wording like MV at cost or loss on sale instead of account names.
questions.fix: Label each entry with the name of the other account.

questions.topic: Advice on opening a farm shop
questions.issue: Many discussed rent and extra finance, and few mentioned the delivery vehicle just bought would no longer be needed.
questions.fix: Use the facts about the existing business and give a clear recommendation.

questions.issue: Many reversed it, left out the opening rent accrued or wrote the wrong word for the bank.
questions.fix: Put opening accrued rent on the debit side and name the bank entry bank.

questions.issue: Very few got full marks because candidates left out the opening difference and added items that need no suspense entry.
questions.fix: Start with the trial balance difference and include only entries that affect suspense.

questions.issue: Candidates left out the starting bank balance, included items that did not affect the bank or reversed the adjustments.
questions.fix: Start from the balance before the errors and add or subtract only bank items in the right direction.

questions.issue: Many knew the formula but picked the wrong figures, and some ignored two decimal places or the percentage sign.
questions.fix: Use profit plus debenture interest over equity plus non-current liabilities and show two decimal places with a percentage sign.

questions.issue: Correct answers were very rare. Many left the cleaning cost out when they worked out what the bags needing cleaning would sell for.
questions.fix: Take the selling price less the cleaning cost, compare it with cost and use the lower figure.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Candidates did well on regular topics such as the cash book and partnerships.
Candidates tend to like the partnership appropriation account, and the current account regularly earned full marks.
Candidates did better on the rent and rates expense account.
Most candidates found one or two points in favour of taking on a bookkeeper and one point against.
mistakes: Candidates used a standard answer for each of the three written questions, without adjusting to each scenario.
Cash book entries went wrong on discounts, and the transfer from bank to cash was often missed.
Interest on drawings was calculated without using the time the drawings were held, and interest on drawings and on capital were mixed up.
Capital balances were wrongly shown in the appropriation account and the current account.
Ledger accounts for depreciation and the provision for doubtful debts had the opening balance missing or placed on the wrong side.
Some answers suggested reducing credit sales to cut irrecoverable debts, which is unrealistic.
fix: Read each written question carefully and write a different answer for each scenario.
Calculate cash discount correctly, record the bank to cash transfer on both sides and check the cash balance is not overdrawn.
Calculate interest on drawings for the months each amount was held, and keep capital out of the appropriation account.
Show the opening balance on each ledger account and bring a balance down.
Suggest realistic ways to reduce irrecoverable debts, not stopping credit sales altogether.

questions.issue: Discount calculations and the transfer from bank to cash were often wrong, sometimes giving an overdrawn cash balance.
questions.fix: Record the contra entry on both sides and treat an overdrawn cash balance as a warning of an error.

questions.issue: Many missed that cash discount was already offered, and wrote about the risk of irrecoverable debts and about liquidity, which did not apply here.
questions.fix: Use the facts about the existing discount and develop each general point with a reason.

questions.issue: Most did not calculate interest on drawings by time held, and some mixed up interest on drawings and on capital.
questions.fix: Work out the interest for the months each amount was held and keep capital balances out.

questions.topic: Advice on converting to a limited company
questions.issue: Candidates wrote a standard answer about adding a new partner, and used vague phrases like higher costs.
questions.fix: Answer the question set, give a reason for each point and make a clear recommendation.

questions.issue: Candidates left out the opening balance, used the wrong side or included motor vehicle balances.
questions.fix: Start with the opening balance, put the charge on the right side and keep asset balances out.

questions.issue: Many did not use their provision from part (b) and omitted the irrecoverable debt.
questions.fix: Show trade receivables less the provision to give a net figure.

questions.issue: Candidates used phrases from the question as account names, and made suspense entries where none were needed.
questions.fix: Use proper account names and only use suspense when the trial balance was affected.

questions.issue: Many assumed sales equalled total receipts, left out purchases, and left out discount received after gross profit.
questions.fix: Find cost of sales first, add the 50 per cent mark-up to reach sales, then add discount received underneath gross profit.

quote.text: candidates do better if they do not jump stages

takeaways: Explain means explain. A list of points, even correct ones, does not earn the marks.
Go through each step of a chain of reasoning, for example higher wages, higher costs, narrower profit gap, lower profit.
Answer the exact question. Candidates lost marks writing about a current account deficit when the question was about the budget, or about the whole economy when it asked about firms.
Learn price elasticity of supply as well as demand. The report says supply seems to be less well understood.
On multiple choice, read the numbers and highlighted words with care. Three of the five hardest questions mixed economics with simple maths.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Five questions were answered correctly by most candidates, across different parts of the syllabus.
mistakes: Candidates mixed up demand with quantity demanded when interpreting an elasticity value.
Over a quarter misread productivity figures, using total output instead of output per worker.
Many read a table of workers as if it showed output.
Many chose a reason to diversify that was actually acceptable when asked for the one that was not.
Some placed the current account of the balance of payments inside the government's finances.
fix: Say quantity demanded changes along the curve when price changes, and demand does not.
Work out output per worker before and after, then calculate the percentage change.
Check what the table counts, workers or output, then add each sector for both years.
Underline words like not in the stem before choosing.
Keep the balance of payments separate from the government budget.

questions.issue: Only 45 per cent were right. Many said demand, not quantity demanded, would change.
questions.fix: With elastic demand, a price cut raises quantity demanded by a bigger percentage, so revenue rises.

questions.issue: Half were right. Over a quarter compared output per worker before with total output after.
questions.fix: Divide total output by workers each time, then find the percentage change.

questions.topic: Workers by sector from a table
questions.issue: Many read the figures as output, not number of workers, and some added up a sector wrongly.
questions.fix: Read what the table measures, then total each sector for each year.

questions.issue: Candidates did not spot the one reason that does not support a wider range of goods.
questions.fix: Test each reason: spreading price risk, less dependence on others and saving resources all support it.

questions.issue: Some thought the current account belongs to the government's finances, and others thought devaluation or higher import duties would cut the surplus.
questions.fix: Ask whether the policy raises imports or exports, then check the effect on the surplus.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Most candidates answered the required number of optional questions and time was well used.
Some candidates gave excellent answers that used economics accurately.
Many drew good maximum price diagrams and explained how lower interest rates raise spending.
Many answered the foreign exchange rate question well, including interest rates and foreign investment.
mistakes: Some wrote long, repetitive answers based on general knowledge instead of economics.
Some stated points without explaining them, which loses marks on Explain questions.
Some described data in a table without interpreting it, or mixed up GDP with GDP per head.
Some gave consequences when asked for causes, or effects on the whole economy when asked about firms.
Candidates confused price elasticity of demand with supply, or named the factors of production when asked for a definition.
fix: Explain each point and move through every step of the reasoning.
Draw a maximum price below equilibrium and show quantity demanded and supplied at that price.
Interpret data. Say what the pattern shows, give evidence and note exceptions.
Check whether the question asks for causes or effects, and who is affected.
Learn separate influences for elasticity of supply and demand, and note which way each pushes.

questions.issue: Some wrote about the effects of the rise, not its causes.
questions.fix: Give causes such as lower interest rates, which encourage borrowing and reduce saving.

questions.issue: Some shifted curves, switched the curves round or drew a production possibility curve.
questions.fix: Keep both curves fixed, draw the cap below equilibrium and mark quantities demanded and supplied.

questions.issue: Some said multinationals might pay lower wages without asking whether that pay could still beat local wages.
questions.fix: Cover both sides and explain each point, such as jobs and tax revenue versus monopoly power.

questions.issue: Some confused which influences make supply elastic or inelastic, and some wrote on demand.
questions.fix: Learn the influences on supply elasticity and say what makes supply more or less responsive.

questions.issue: Some asserted it would cut the exchange rate with no explanation and changed the question.
questions.fix: Link a larger money supply to higher total demand, then weigh growth against inflation and imports.

questions.issue: Some wrote about the economy in general, and a weak sample answer listed effects without explaining.
questions.fix: Focus on firms. Explain how higher costs can cut profits, one step at a time.

questions.issue: Some confused retirement with unemployment and wrote about demand for some products only.
questions.fix: Cover total demand and the labour force, and link them to growth.

questions.issue: Some wrote about the current account deficit, answering a different question.
questions.fix: Link supply-side measures to government spending and tax revenue, and note possible costs.

quote.text: reversed reasoning and instead explain mechanisms accurately

takeaways: Do not answer an opposite question by flipping your earlier sentence. Explain the actual mechanism, for example why a policy could lower a measure, not only raise it.
Explain every point you list. Naming measures or reasons without saying how they work earns little.
Discussion questions need both sides and a conclusion. On the income tax question, many answers argued only one side.
Interpret data. Say what pattern it shows and use figures as evidence, not just copy them out.
On multiple choice, the weaker questions often used graphs and tables, so practise reading data and doing the sums.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Eighteen questions were answered well.
Candidates knew micro topics better than macro topics.
mistakes: Weaker questions usually involved data in graphs or tables.
Candidates thought unemployment reduces the quantity of labour available, when it only means labour is unused.
Many mixed up a move along a production possibility curve with moving to a higher curve.
Many thought a subsidy cuts the price by the whole amount at the same quantity.
Candidates mixed up the central bank's role with commercial bank loans.
fix: Remember unemployment means labour is idle, not that it has gone.
Only more resources or better technology move the economy to a higher curve.
After a subsidy, show a lower price and a higher quantity, with the benefit shared.
Link the central bank to price stability and keep commercial bank loans separate.
Take inflation away from nominal growth to get real growth.

questions.topic: Moving to a higher production possibility curve
questions.issue: Many picked options that only use existing labour more or switch output type.
questions.fix: Look for an increase in the quantity or quality of resources.

questions.issue: Many chose the answer with the same quantity and a price fall equal to the full subsidy.
questions.fix: Show a higher quantity traded, with the price benefit shared by buyer and seller.

questions.issue: Many chose loan facilities, which commercial banks provide.
questions.fix: Link the central bank to price stability, which helps firms plan.

questions.issue: Candidates thought average fixed cost stays constant, and misread average total cost.
questions.fix: Spread the fixed cost over more output, so average fixed cost falls. Check variable cost per unit.

questions.issue: Many chose domestic policies like minimum wages and deregulation.
questions.fix: Pick measures that change trade directly, such as a weaker currency or tariffs.

questions.topic: Demand side policy and inflation over time
questions.issue: Many missed that inflation may rise in the short run and ease in the long run with better skills.
questions.fix: Separate short run demand effects from long run productivity effects.

questions.issue: Candidates looked at one figure and ignored the other.
questions.fix: Subtract inflation from nominal growth in every option.

questions.issue: Many chose large surpluses in both income parts, which would not give a balance.
questions.fix: Add the four parts and find the combination that cancels the trade surplus.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Candidates showed clear knowledge of core ideas such as the economic problem.
Candidates supported data answers with accurate evidence and explained fiscal and supply-side policy well.
Many used elasticity ideas such as substitutes, income and luxury status.
Candidates produced developed chains of reasoning and balanced extended answers with conclusions.
mistakes: Candidates needed a clearer grasp of income distribution between countries.
A few copied data without saying how it supported the trend.
Some just reversed their earlier reasoning when asked for the opposite effect.
Some wrote about how price changes affect demand, not about what determines elasticity.
Many answers on fixed exchange rates were simple statements such as that the government sets them.
fix: Interpret a table. Name the relationship, give figures and note any exception.
Explain the mechanism both ways, not just the reverse of your last sentence.
List factors that determine elasticity, such as substitutes, and say whether they make demand more or less elastic.
Develop a point about fixed rates by saying what limits policy or what it gives firms.
Give reasons for and against, then write a short conclusion.

questions.issue: Many named a reason but could not explain its effect on land.
questions.fix: Pick one cause and show how it harms soil or yields.

questions.topic: Capital equipment and the current account
questions.issue: Some described productivity but not the effect on exports, imports and the deficit, and a few confused it with government debt.
questions.fix: Go from productivity to costs, then competitiveness, then trade flows.

questions.issue: Some left out axes or equilibrium labels, or moved the wrong curve.
questions.fix: Label axes and curves, shift demand only and mark the new equilibrium.

questions.issue: Some said the relationship was positive, and a few copied figures with no explanation.
questions.fix: State the direction, use figures as evidence and link income to affording necessities.

questions.topic: Fiscal policy and a development index
questions.issue: Some reversed their earlier reasoning for a lower value, and wrote vaguely about living standards.
questions.fix: Tie fiscal policy to each part of the index, such as schooling, life expectancy and income.

questions.topic: Future price elasticity of a commodity
questions.issue: Some wrote that a high price cuts demand, which is not about elasticity.
questions.fix: Apply determinants such as substitutes and luxury status, and say how they may change.

questions.issue: Many simply said the government sets the rate, and some switched to multinational investment.
questions.fix: Cover certainty for firms and limits on other aims, and contrast with floating rates.

questions.issue: Some said they are goods the government provides, or mixed them with merit goods.
questions.fix: Define them as non rivalrous and non excludable.

quote.text: read the wording of the questions very carefully

takeaways: Read every word of the question. Marks were lost by treating a market as the whole economy, or by writing about the wrong tax or the wrong deficit.
In Section A, use the source material. Several answers drifted into outside facts instead of using the data given.
Count how many answers are asked for. Many questions wanted exactly two points, and some candidates gave four or only one.
Eight mark questions need two sides with explanation. A conclusion only helps if it adds something new.
Explain each point, not just name it. A reason with no development misses the development mark.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Five questions were answered correctly by most candidates, across different topics.
mistakes: Many candidates thought a rise in both demand and supply gives a definite price change.
Many misread price inelastic demand data.
Many forgot that a move to more capital is least likely when interest rates rise.
Candidates did not link a firm making fewer products to more specialisation.
Candidates mixed up what a central bank would buy or sell to make its currency appreciate.
fix: When demand and supply both rise, say quantity rises and price is uncertain.
Test elasticity by comparing the percentage change in price with the percentage change in quantity.
Link capital use to borrowing and interest rates.
Connect narrower product range to more specialisation.
To raise its currency, a central bank must buy its own currency in the market.

questions.issue: Most chose a definite price move. Both curves shifting right makes price uncertain.
questions.fix: State that quantity rises. Price depends on which shift is bigger.

questions.issue: Many picked options with elastic demand, which do not fit the data.
questions.fix: Calculate percentage changes in price and quantity and compare them.

questions.issue: Only a third saw that rising interest rates make borrowing for capital less likely.
questions.fix: Ask which factor would discourage a firm from borrowing to invest.

questions.issue: Many chose options that would not change specialisation.
questions.fix: Look for a firm narrowing its range of products.

questions.issue: Candidates mixed up the amount and the direction of the central bank's action.
questions.fix: Read the diagram to see how much of its own currency must be bought.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Five questions were answered correctly by most candidates.
mistakes: The majority mixed up occupational immobility with geographical immobility.
Many compared absolute wage gaps and not relative wage gaps.
Some candidates thought rising average cost after a merger came from economies of scale.
Over a third counted only people in work when finding the labour force.
Candidates confused cause and effect when linking a current account surplus to the exchange rate.
fix: Occupational means skills, while geographical means location.
Compare wage ratios, not the size of the pound or dollar gap.
After a merger, rising average cost is a coordination problem, not a saving.
Labour force means people working plus those looking for work.
Work out whether the surplus is the cause or the consequence before choosing.

questions.issue: Most chose geographic immobility instead of lacking the right skills.
questions.fix: Check whether the barrier is about skills or about moving location.

questions.issue: Many chose the biggest absolute gap, not the smallest female to male ratio.
questions.fix: Divide female pay by male pay and pick the lowest ratio.

questions.issue: A large minority said the cost rise came from economies of scale.
questions.fix: Rising average cost fits coordination and communication problems.

questions.issue: Over a third counted only the employed.
questions.fix: Add those working and those actively seeking work.

questions.issue: Around a quarter said the problem was that the goods are not exported, and another quarter that farming is excluded.
questions.fix: The issue is that the value of unsold output is unknown.

questions.issue: A little over a third chose the cause as the effect.
questions.fix: A surplus comes with strong demand for exports, which can cut unemployment.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Five questions were answered correctly by most candidates.
mistakes: Most chose price inelastic when given a negative elasticity value that was less than minus one.
Many picked the wrong point on a cost curve when asked for diseconomies of scale.
Many read a cost table as if it showed average cost.
A third thought uncertainty would arise from a known tax rate.
A quarter of candidates thought that more money in the economy lowers prices.
fix: Ignore the minus sign. Compare the size of the figure with one.
Diseconomies of scale are where average cost rises as output rises.
Divide total cost by output to get average total cost.
Match the drawback to the situation described, such as less work at high tax rates.
Link technology to lower prices, and more money or higher costs to higher prices.

questions.issue: More than half chose inelastic, possibly put off by the minus sign.
questions.fix: Use the size of the value. Above one means elastic.

questions.issue: The most common wrong answer was the point where cost fell fastest.
questions.fix: Find the part of the curve where average cost rises with output.

questions.issue: The most common wrong answer may have come from reading the rising totals without working out the average.
questions.fix: Add fixed and variable cost, divide by output, then compare.

questions.issue: A little over a third chose uncertainty, though a known tax rate does not create it.
questions.fix: Less work means less income to tax, so tax revenue is not at its highest.

questions.issue: A quarter said a bigger money supply causes deflation, and similar shares chose higher employment or higher costs.
questions.fix: Technology that lowers costs is the likely cause. The others push prices up.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Many calculated the percentage correctly and nearly all gave two external benefits.
Candidates were generally good at explaining two reasons for cutting reliance on oil.
Most scored full marks on drawing a supply shift diagram.
Strong answers used the data to describe a negative relationship and explained the exception.
mistakes: A common error was counting a product sold in a market as an external benefit.
Most candidates did not mention exports or give a precise current account effect.
Many added a text commentary, and some shifted the wrong curve or drew two diagrams.
Weaker answers described each data point separately, and some called the relationship indirectly proportional.
Part (b) answers often lacked development or missed that two points were asked, and in 4(a) numerous candidates gave four aims.
fix: Use only benefits that go to third parties, not to buyers and sellers in the market.
Say that more tourists raise exports, then name the surplus or deficit change.
Draw one diagram, label both axes and curves, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.
Describe the overall pattern with the data, then explain the exception.
Give exactly the number of answers asked and develop each one.

questions.issue: A common error was counting timber, which is sold in the market.
questions.fix: Pick benefits like cleaner air and flood protection, which go to third parties.

questions.issue: Most gave only a vague answer and missed exports.
questions.fix: Say tourist spending is an export of services and improves the current account.

questions.issue: Many missed the equilibrium shift, swapped curves or added text.
questions.fix: Label everything, shift supply right and mark both equilibria.

questions.issue: Weaker answers listed values for each country with no link between them.
questions.fix: State the direction of the relationship, use two examples and explain the exception.

questions.issue: Weaker answers listed factors that raise total cost but not average cost.
questions.fix: Give at least three economies and diseconomies, each tied to average cost.

questions.issue: Some gave rewards to labour or enterprise.
questions.fix: Learn the rewards: interest for capital and rent for land.

questions.issue: Weaker answers just described supply rising and falling, not the factor causing it.
questions.fix: Name causes such as cost changes, weather or subsidies, then show the effect on supply and price.

questions.issue: Many described strong and weak currency, not the floating system itself.
questions.fix: Cover automatic correction of imbalances against the risk and uncertainty for traders and investors.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Most candidates did the calculation accurately and many used the source well.
Most candidates explained how tourism could cause pollution or another external cost.
Many answered the data question on the link between two variables well.
The (c) parts were generally answered better, with strong analysis.
mistakes: A few made calculation slips, such as the wrong unit, or confused a budget deficit with a current account deficit.
Some treated farm products as if they were land.
Many explained a pollution effect without saying why it is an external cost.
Many added a written explanation when only a diagram was requested, and some shifted the supply curve the wrong way.
Some copied the source material for the deflation question without interpreting it.
fix: Include the unit in your answer and check it makes sense.
Land means natural resources, not what is grown or built on it.
Say why a cost falls on people who are not buyers or sellers.
When the question says draw, give the diagram only.
