Check the bank loan and retained earnings entries when you rebuild a statement.
Production cost of goods completed is the transfer price less the factory profit.

questions.issue: Some gave general goodwill explanations that did not relate to the scenario, and could not discuss splitting the shares.
questions.fix: Tie every explanation to the facts about each person and the share split.

questions.topic: Statement of financial position after the changes
questions.issue: Some got the bank loan wrong, missed the movement in retained earnings, or both.
questions.fix: Update each equity and liability item, including retained earnings, after the changes.

questions.issue: Some identified IAS37 and a contingent asset but did not develop the change in treatment.
questions.fix: Name the standard, then explain what changes in the accounts and why.

questions.issue: Some candidates left out elements, and some omitted the bank overdraft.
questions.fix: List every asset and liability, including overdrafts, before calculating the closing fund.

questions.issue: Some candidates gave only one or two consequences, while the best answers gave three or four.
questions.fix: Aim for three or four separate consequences.

questions.issue: Candidates posted the opening balance and transfer but not the closing balance correctly.
questions.fix: Post the opening, the movement and the closing balance, and carry the movement to the statement of profit or loss.

questions.issue: Some gave only two or three valid reasons, while the best answers gave four or five.
questions.fix: Give as many distinct valid reasons as the marks suggest.

papers.title: Cost and management accounting
well: Some candidates showed a good knowledge of a wide range of the syllabus.
Activity based costing, budgets and standard costing calculations were well understood.
Many candidates produced fully labelled production budgets.
mistakes: Written answers did not relate to the scenario.
Evaluation answers were not balanced and did not give the required decision.
Fixed overheads were not dealt with correctly in the costing statement, and some candidates did not turn total overheads into overheads per unit.
Some candidates left out the direct costs or the mark-up when they worked out selling prices.
Variances had correct numbers but candidates did not state favourable or adverse.
Opening and closing inventory were reversed in the production budget.
fix: Refer to the scenario facts in each written answer.
Balance both sides and give a decision that the facts support.
Use all the cost drivers when you calculate overheads for each product, then convert to a figure per unit.
Add the direct costs to the overhead per unit to get total unit cost, then add the mark-up to reach the selling price.
Write favourable or adverse next to every variance.

questions.issue: Candidates described the allocation but did not conclude whether the method was suitable.
questions.fix: End with a clear judgement about the suitability of the method.

questions.issue: Some apportioned only some of the costs and did not convert total overheads into a figure per unit.
questions.fix: Use all the cost drivers and divide by units to get overhead per unit.

questions.issue: Some gave a decision without using the scenario data fully.
questions.fix: Weigh both sides using the data given, then justify your decision.

questions.issue: Some calculated only some months of inventory and converted only to money, not to kilos.
questions.fix: Work out every month's inventory, then convert purchases into both kilos and dollars.

questions.issue: Some candidates got the number right but did not say whether it was favourable or adverse.
questions.fix: Label every variance as favourable or adverse.

questions.issue: Some gave a calculation and a decision but too few relevant points for each option.
questions.fix: Make several points about each option and support your decision with them.

quote.text: Marks will always be awarded for valid workings

takeaways: Show clear workings on every calculation. The report says valid workings always earn marks, and no workings earns nothing.
Be careful with the word eliminate. Controls and checks make errors and fraud easier to detect or prevent, not impossible.
Write labels in full with up to date terms, such as profit for the year. Add correct dates and details in ledger accounts.
Written answers need development. One or two word answers seldom earn marks, especially when the command word is explain.
Advice answers should use the scenario, give both sides and finish with a clear decision.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Almost three quarters of candidates got questions 1, 27, 28 and 29 right.
More than half of candidates scored 16 or more correct answers.
mistakes: Candidates believed there is an account called bank overdraft in the general ledger.
Some assumed a contra entry had been duplicated in both control accounts when the question did not say so.
Only some candidates saw that an error in a book of prime entry carries through to the ledger, so the trial balance does not catch it.
In a purchases ledger control account, some included cash sales and returns inwards.
fix: Remember that an overdraft is just the bank account with a negative balance. There is no separate overdraft account.
Think through how each posting moves from a book of prime entry into the ledger accounts.
Only use what the question tells you, and do not assume extra errors.
When you restate a balance, leave out items that do not belong, such as cash sales in a purchases control account.

questions.issue: Many chose options that posted to a bank overdraft account, which does not exist. Fewer than one in five chose the key.
questions.fix: Treat an overdraft as a credit balance on the bank account.

questions.issue: Some assumed the contra was duplicated in both control accounts. Only some saw that a mistake made in a book of prime entry carries forward.
questions.fix: Use only the facts given. A book of prime entry error will not be revealed by the trial balance.

questions.issue: Candidates were caught by two irrelevant items, cash sales and returns inwards. Only 30 per cent chose the key.
questions.fix: Include only credit purchases and ignore anything that relates to sales.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Question 22 was straightforward and 88 per cent chose the key.
More than half of candidates scored 14 or more correct answers.
mistakes: Just over half of candidates thought a bank reconciliation would eliminate fraud.
Candidates mixed up the depreciation not yet charged and the profit on disposal.
Many thought accurate splitting of costs into fixed and variable was a decision making aid in CVP, not a basic requirement.
fix: Watch the word eliminate. It is very definite, while easier to detect or easier to prevent is more realistic.
When correcting profit, think through every item that raises or lowers the original figure.
Learn the main assumptions, advantages and limitations of CVP analysis.

questions.issue: Just over half picked an option saying a reconciliation eliminates fraud. Only a quarter chose the key.
questions.fix: A reconciliation may reduce the chance of fraud but cannot guarantee to remove it.

questions.topic: Profit on sale of an asset
questions.issue: Answers split between the depreciation not yet charged, the profit on sale and the correct net of the two.
questions.fix: Reduce the profit on sale by depreciation not yet charged for the months before the sale.

questions.issue: Many chose an option that is a basic requirement of CVP, not a decision making aid.
questions.fix: Separate what CVP needs as an assumption from what it is used for in practice.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 1, 2, 7, 14, 19, 23 and 29 were answered correctly by most candidates.
More than half of candidates scored 18 or more correct answers.
No question caused severe difficulty, because at least 30 per cent chose the key for each.
mistakes: Candidates counted replacement of wheels on a car as capital expenditure.
Candidates treated a bank error as an item to adjust in the cash book.
Some assumed no interest applies on a partner loan when the agreement is silent.
Some thought an actual activity level below budget causes over absorption.
fix: Ask whether spending improves the asset. Replacement and repair are revenue expenditure.
Only adjust the cash book for items that need an entry in the business's own books.
Remember that the Partnership Act applies when the agreement does not mention a point, including interest on a loan.
Think through how a lower volume affects absorbed overheads.

questions.issue: Many included replacing parts on a car, which is repair, not an improvement.
questions.fix: Count only the purchase and the enhancement as capital.

questions.issue: Candidates split between two answers because a bank error was wrongly included.
questions.fix: Ignore errors made by the bank in its own books.

questions.issue: Some chose zero interest because loans were not mentioned.
questions.fix: When the agreement says nothing, the Partnership Act applies and gives 5 per cent.

questions.topic: Over and under absorption of overheads
questions.issue: Candidates mixed up statements and thought lower activity would cause over absorption.
questions.fix: Think through what happens to absorbed overheads when activity is below budget.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: The majority gave four provisions of the Partnership Act and three disadvantages of full records correctly.
Candidates explained a difference between capital and revenue reserves well.
Many discussed finance options well and reached an appropriate conclusion.
Just in time inventory management was generally well answered.
mistakes: Few candidates could calculate closing inventory, because they did not adjust sales to cost price.
Abbreviations and old terminology appeared in financial statements.
Many could not work out other receivables, other payables or opening equity.
Statements of changes in equity used dates instead of narratives and no narrative on the total line.
Suspense accounts had poor details and brought the balance down to the next year.
Absorption costing statements lacked the first month's closing inventory and the under absorption.
fix: Show clear workings for every calculation, because workings earn marks when the answer is wrong.
Convert sales to cost price when you work out closing inventory from incomplete records.
Use current terminology and write labels in full.
Describe each equity transaction, such as bonus issue, in the details column.
Label contribution and profit in a marginal costing statement.

questions.issue: Very few candidates calculated it correctly. The common mistake was not reducing sales to cost price.
questions.fix: Adjust sales to cost price first, then find the closing inventory.

questions.issue: Many found three figures hard to work out: opening equity, other payables and other receivables.
questions.fix: Build each missing figure with workings before placing it in the statement.

questions.issue: Many mishandled a fall in land value and used dates instead of narratives such as bonus issue.
questions.fix: Write the narrative for each line and give the final total line a date.

questions.issue: Marks were lost for poor details, and some brought the balance down to the next year.
questions.fix: Write clear details and do not bring the balance down to the next year.

questions.issue: Only well prepared candidates calculated it correctly.
questions.fix: List every error with an add or subtract and show workings.

questions.issue: Many did not work out the first month's closing inventory or record the under absorption of overheads.
questions.fix: Calculate closing inventory and record under absorbed overheads.

questions.issue: This kind of statement was unfamiliar, and only well prepared candidates scored marks.
questions.fix: Practise reconciling the profit under absorption costing to marginal costing.

questions.issue: Answers were vague and did not say how closing inventory is valued.
questions.fix: State exactly how each method values closing inventory.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: Well prepared candidates gained very good marks on the statement of profit or loss.
Many candidates gave valid revenue reserve examples and valid factors that cause depreciation.
Most scored five or six out of six on apportioning overheads.
Many were familiar with control accounts and answered the sales ledger control account well.
mistakes: Many candidates could not value closing inventory, so cost of sales was hard.
Labels used abbreviations and old terms such as net profit instead of profit for the year.
Ledger accounts for vehicles had basic double entry errors and missing dates and labels.
Some described the two depreciation methods without answering why reducing balance suits vehicles.
Overhead rates ignored two decimal places and the per machine hour or labour hour label.
Over absorption and under absorption were confused, and direct labour was harder than direct materials.
fix: Write labels in full and use new terminology, such as profit for the year.
Add dates and clear details to every ledger entry.
Answer why the method suits the asset and relate it to the matching concept.
State rates to two decimal places with the unit.
Reuse your earlier figures and include all the departments' overheads in a price calculation.

questions.topic: Statement of profit or loss with adjustments
questions.issue: Cost of sales was hardest because closing inventory was often wrong, and labels were abbreviated.
questions.fix: Work out closing inventory carefully and write labels in full.

questions.issue: Presentation was generally good, but some wrote only dates in the details column.
questions.fix: Write the full detail of each transaction.

questions.topic: Bonus issue or new issue advice
questions.issue: Some lost marks by giving one point twice, once for each option.
questions.fix: Give separate points for each option, then advise.

questions.issue: Many showed inadequate double entry and lost marks for missing dates and labels.
questions.fix: Practise the disposal entries and date every line.

questions.issue: Some only described the two methods.
questions.fix: Explain why reducing balance suits vehicles and use the matching concept.

questions.issue: Few were totally correct and many did not attempt it.
questions.fix: Attempt the schedule using the corrected figures.

questions.issue: Most figures were right, but many ignored two decimal places or the unit.
questions.fix: Show two decimal places and write per machine hour or per labour hour.

questions.topic: Selling price for a special order
questions.issue: It was generally poorly answered because earlier figures were not used and some overheads were missed.
questions.fix: Add the direct cost and both departments' overheads to get total cost. For a 30 per cent margin, gross profit is 30/70 of that cost.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: Well prepared candidates used current terminology, correct dates and correct details in their ledger accounts.
Candidates were successful on trade receivables days and trade payables days, including the formulas.
Candidates gave good disadvantages of computerised systems and good ways to secure data.
Break-even calculations were well answered, and revised profit questions scored well for those who knew fixed and variable costs.
mistakes: Candidates struggled with closing accruals and prepayments in administrative expenses.
Net trade receivables were not shown after the write off and the allowance.
Ledger accounts for share capital, share premium and retained earnings were weak, with wrong details.
Candidates did not work out cost of sales correctly when finding closing inventory from inventory turnover.
Differences between marginal and absorption costing, and direct and indirect costs, were vague.
Some definitions of margin of safety were not precise enough.
fix: Check accruals and prepayments at the end of the year.
Show net trade receivables after deducting the write off and the allowance.
Practise basic double entry in equity accounts and write the correct detail for each transaction.
Learn the inventory turnover formula and work out cost of sales properly.
In differences, explain both items rather than describing one.

questions.issue: Administrative expenses were the hardest part because closing accruals and prepayments were mishandled.
questions.fix: Adjust each expense for both accruals and prepayments.

questions.issue: New terminology was missing, and net trade receivables were not shown.
questions.fix: Deduct the write off and the allowance to show net trade receivables.

questions.issue: Many could not work out cost of sales and results were very mixed.
questions.fix: Work out cost of sales correctly first, then use the turnover figure to find closing inventory.

questions.issue: Candidates showed a lack of basic double entry, and used wrong details.
questions.fix: Write the correct details for each transaction and put entries on the right side.

questions.issue: Several answers were vague and described only one system.
questions.fix: Write a clear difference that mentions both.

questions.issue: Some definitions were too loose to earn the mark.
questions.fix: Give a precise definition, not a loose one.

questions.issue: Some were unsure and gave answers without enough depth.
questions.fix: Give three clear situations and explain how marginal costing helps in each.

papers.title: Financial accounting
well: Candidates performed reasonably well, with Question 2 the best answered.
Earnings per share was calculated correctly by most.
Most candidates advised as asked and backed it up with one or two relevant comments.
Statements of cash flows were reasonable, and most used the IAS7 format.
mistakes: Few candidates produced a fully correct revised profit, because a damages claim was included and sale or return goods were treated wrongly.
Some price earnings answers gave a money value, not the ratio.
Candidates named three measures but did not develop them enough to earn the second mark.
Realisation accounts left out the vehicle a partner took over and included the bank balance. Capital accounts mishandled the vehicle and left out the bank entries.
Journals omitted or miscalculated goodwill, and some used ledger account format.
Cash flow statements lost marks for leaving out depreciation, mistreating tax paid and interest paid, and miscalculating dividends paid.
fix: Check each adjustment to profit and decide if it belongs.
Give each ratio in the correct format and two decimal places.
Develop each measure with a reason to earn the second mark.
Include the vehicle taken over and leave out the bank balance in a realisation account.
Use journal format for journal entries.

questions.issue: Few were fully correct, as some included a damages claim and few treated sale or return goods correctly.
questions.fix: Work out the correct effect of each adjustment before changing profit.

questions.issue: Some gave a money value, but most showed the change properly and to two decimal places.
questions.fix: State the ratio in the correct form with two decimal places.

questions.topic: Ways to lower the gearing ratio
questions.issue: A significant number gave three measures, but few developed them enough for the second mark.
questions.fix: Add a reason or explanation to each measure.

questions.topic: Reasons for preparing a statement of profit or loss
questions.issue: Only a few gave three reasons, and some gave none.
questions.fix: Learn why a limited company prepares this statement and give three reasons.

questions.issue: Candidates left out the vehicle taken over by a partner and included the bank balance.
questions.fix: Include assets taken over and leave out the bank balance.

questions.issue: Many omitted or miscalculated goodwill and some answered as a ledger account.
questions.fix: Calculate goodwill and present the answer as a journal.

questions.issue: Marks were lost for leaving out depreciation, mistreating tax paid and interest paid, and miscalculating dividends paid.
questions.fix: Put each entry in the correct section, include depreciation and check the tax, interest and dividend figures.

questions.topic: How shareholders view changes in capital employed
questions.issue: No question on the paper was answered worse, as few considered each element of capital employed.
questions.fix: Consider each element of capital employed in turn.

papers.title: Financial accounting
well: Performance overall was satisfactory, and Question 2 was answered best.
Nearly all candidates gave the required advice on the club question.
Most candidates prepared the cash flow statement using the IAS7 sections.
In the first part, many made the adjustments correctly.
mistakes: Very few correct statements of profit or loss, as few used the correct cost of production and closing inventory.
Many left the year's transfer to income and expenditure out of the life membership fund calculation.
A significant number ignored comparing the accumulated fund at the start and end of the year.
Few adjusted for the life membership fund, entered life membership fees, or entered the deficit.
Candidates did not account for depreciation or the rights issue proceeds in the cash flow statement, and many left out opening and closing bank balances.
Some gave calculations when the question asked for none.
fix: Use the correct cost of production and closing inventory in the statement of profit or loss.
Compare the opening accumulated fund with the closing one, and adjust for the life membership fund.
Label the balancing figure as instructed, such as other operating expenses.
Enter the opening and closing bank balances in the cash flow statement.
Read the instruction. If no calculations are asked for, explain in words.

questions.topic: Statement of profit or loss with factory profit
questions.issue: Few were fully correct, and few had the right figures for cost of production, closing inventory and administrative expenses.
questions.fix: Take each figure from the right working and check administrative expenses.

questions.issue: Only a few justified the decision well enough for more than two of four extra marks.
questions.fix: Develop points for stopping as well as for not stopping.

questions.issue: Many left out the year's transfer from the fund to income and expenditure.
questions.fix: Take the year's transfer to income and expenditure off the fund before giving the closing balance.

questions.issue: Very few correct, because many ignored comparing start and end and the life membership balance.
questions.fix: Compare the fund at both dates and include the life membership balance.

questions.issue: Many omitted tournament profit and life membership fees, and ignored the instructed label.
questions.fix: Include every income item and use the label given in the question.

questions.issue: Few accounted for depreciation, and many did not enter the opening and closing bank balances.
questions.fix: Include depreciation, rights issue proceeds and both bank balances.

questions.issue: Few explained the rise by setting higher profit against the changed number of shares, and some gave calculations.
questions.fix: Explain in words how profit and the number of shares affect earnings per share.

questions.issue: Few earned both marks. Some believed the issue would bring in cash, and few explained the effect on reserves.
questions.fix: A bonus issue brings in no cash. Explain what it does to the reserves.

papers.title: Financial accounting
well: Performance was very good across all three questions.
Working capital cycle calculations had a high number of fully correct answers.
Club subscriptions accounts were well prepared and a high number gave two acceptable ways to improve a club's performance.
Nearly all candidates gave the required advice.
mistakes: Machinery cost was derived incorrectly in the non-current asset calculations.
Some did not follow the prescribed format for the schedule and mishandled the revaluation.
Candidates found an implication for the auditors more easily than one for the directors.
Written advice was often generic rather than applied to the scenario.
Some gave the formula when it was not required, and some did not give one decimal place.
fix: Work out the cost of machinery carefully, and treat the revaluation correctly in the schedule.
Follow the format the question prescribes.
Consider every person affected, including the directors as well as the auditors.
Apply advice to the facts of the scenario.
Give the ratio to the stated number of decimal places and skip the formula if it is not asked for.

questions.issue: The most common error was the cost of machinery.
questions.fix: Derive cost carefully before accumulated depreciation and carrying value.

questions.issue: The most common error was the treatment of the revaluation.
questions.fix: Use the prescribed format and treat the revaluation properly.

questions.issue: Most gave an implication for the auditors, but not as many gave one for the directors.
questions.fix: State an implication for each group the question names.

questions.issue: Some did not account for existing life members at the start of the year.
questions.fix: Include members from the start of the year.

questions.issue: The most common error was omitted or wrong treatment of the written off subscription.
questions.fix: Include the written off subscription correctly.

questions.issue: Most gave the effect but few gave a good reason.
questions.fix: Explain the reason, not just the effect.

questions.issue: Points were often generic and not applied to the scenario.
questions.fix: Use the facts about the club.

questions.issue: Lost marks usually came from a wrong inventory turnover figure.
questions.fix: Calculate inventory turnover carefully along with receivables and payables.

papers.title: Cost and management accounting
well: Candidates dealt correctly with cash and credit sales in the cash budget.
Many gave a balanced justification by considering both options in the advice questions.
Many candidates stated one benefit of variance analysis, and the sales price variance was often correct.
Strong responses supported decisions with calculations for both suppliers.
mistakes: Weak answers gave purposes of a budget in general instead of a cash budget.
Most could not work out the payments to suppliers, and depreciation was handled wrongly in operating expenses.
Candidates showed three months in the budgeted statement of profit or loss rather than the period.
Few correct entries for discount received and irrecoverable debt.
Very few calculated the sales volume variance or the fixed overhead total variance.
A high number ignored the requirement to calculate other relevant variances.
fix: Answer the question for a cash budget, not budgets in general.
Work out payments to suppliers from the information given and treat depreciation correctly in operating expenses.
Show one figure for the whole period in a budgeted statement.
Practise sales volume and fixed overhead variances.
When asked for sub-variances, calculate them and then explain the total variance.

questions.issue: Weak responses gave two purposes of a budget in general.
questions.fix: Name purposes that apply to a cash budget specifically.

questions.issue: Few were fully correct. Most could not find payments to suppliers and some mishandled depreciation.
questions.fix: Work out supplier payments, and treat depreciation correctly when finding operating expenses.

questions.topic: Budgeted statement of profit or loss
questions.issue: Many showed three separate months and few had correct discount received and irrecoverable debt.
questions.fix: Show the whole period and include each item.

questions.issue: A few gave two benefits and many gave one.
questions.fix: Give two distinct benefits.

questions.issue: Few could calculate the sales volume variance or the fixed overhead total variance.
questions.fix: Practise these two variances with worked examples.

questions.issue: Many ignored the request for other relevant variances.
questions.fix: Calculate the sub-variances and explain the total variance.

questions.issue: Strong responses used calculations and arguments about both suppliers.
questions.fix: Support your decision with figures and a point on each supplier.

papers.title: Cost and management accounting
well: Question 1 was the best answered question.
Most candidates showed they understood activity based costing and gave a reasonable explanation.
Many gave two or three acceptable advantages in a short question.
Production budgets were reasonable, with many fully correct.
mistakes: Some explained advantages and disadvantages of ABC instead of explaining the method.
Candidates calculated a rate for each product instead of one overhead absorption rate.
Some posted the whole fixed overhead figure to each product, the mark-up was applied wrongly and some used a unit basis.
Supervision cost was wrongly treated in the ABC allocation.
Cash sales were mixed with credit sales in the trade receivables budget, and the opening balance was not carried forward.
Discount allowed was left out or put in the wrong month, and production units were not carried into the purchases budget.
fix: Explain what ABC is before you weigh its pros and cons.
Calculate one absorption rate when the question asks for a single rate.
Absorb fixed overheads into each product with the absorption rate, then apply the mark-up to total cost.
Carry the closing balance forward as the next opening balance and place discount in the right month.
Use your own earlier figures in the budget and in the advice.

questions.issue: Some listed advantages and disadvantages rather than explaining it.
questions.fix: Explain how the method works first.

questions.issue: Many calculated one for each product, when a single rate was needed.
questions.fix: Use one rate for the whole business as the question asks.

questions.topic: Budgeted profit statement for two products
questions.issue: Many gave each product the whole fixed overhead figure and misapplied the mark-up.
questions.fix: Absorb fixed overheads into each product with the absorption rate, then apply the mark-up to each total cost.

questions.issue: The most common error was the supervision cost, and some reused revenue from the earlier method.
questions.fix: Allocate each cost by its driver and recalculate revenue.

questions.issue: Many ignored the instruction to support their answer by referring to parts (c) and (d).
questions.fix: Refer to the selling prices and figures from the earlier parts.

questions.topic: Trade receivables budget for two months
questions.issue: Many did not bring forward the opening balance, and some included cash sales or omitted the discount allowed.
questions.fix: Carry forward each closing balance, include credit sales only and apply discount in the right month.

questions.issue: Some used sales units, mixed dollars, units and kilos, or ignored inventory.
questions.fix: Start from production units and adjust for opening and closing inventory in consistent units.

papers.title: Cost and management accounting
well: Performance was very good, with Question 2 the best answered.
Many fully correct statements were produced in the first question.
Net cash flow statements for both models were well prepared.
Net present value work was excellent, and the report found no common errors.
mistakes: The fixed overhead was the most common error in the flexible budget statement.
Far fewer candidates calculated the sales volume variance and the fixed overhead volume variance.
Reconciliation statements treated variances in the wrong direction and left out the variances for direct materials and direct labour.
Some cash flow answers ignored the improvement cost when working out depreciation, or did not cap year two sales at maximum production capacity.
Not as many handled the additional revenue correctly when finding its net present value.
fix: Take extra care with the fixed overhead line in the flexible budget statement.
Practise both fixed overhead variances and the sales volume variance.
Check whether each variance increases or decreases profit before using it in a reconciliation, and include every variance.
Work out depreciation on the purchase price plus the improvement cost before you take it out of fixed overheads, and cap sales at maximum capacity.
Discount the additional revenue properly in a net present value calculation.

questions.issue: Many got full marks. Fixed overhead was where answers most often went wrong.
questions.fix: Take extra care with the fixed overhead line.

questions.topic: Sales volume and fixed overhead variances
questions.issue: Sales price variance was well done, but fewer calculated sales volume and fixed overhead volume variances.
questions.fix: Practise these two variances.

questions.issue: Errors included variances in the wrong direction and missing direct materials and direct labour variances.
questions.fix: Include every variance and check its direction before adjusting.

questions.topic: Net cash flows for two models
questions.issue: Some ignored the improvement cost when working out depreciation, or missed the production capacity limit in year two.
questions.fix: Base depreciation on the purchase price plus the improvement cost, remove it from fixed overheads and cap sales at capacity.

questions.topic: Net present value of additional revenue
questions.issue: Most discounted the improvement cost correctly, but fewer handled the additional revenue.
questions.fix: Discount each year's additional revenue with the right factor.

quote.text: evaluation must compare and contrast the preceding analysis

takeaways: Read the command words and any underlined or highlighted words twice. Many marks were lost across AS and A Level by answering a different question from the one set.
A diagram or formula on its own only earns knowledge marks. You must explain what it shows to reach analysis.
Evaluation needs a judgement that uses your earlier points. Repeating them or listing one sentence comments stays in the bottom level.
If the question asks for a diagram, draw the right one and label it fully. The wrong diagram caps your level.
On multiple choice, work out the answer with the numbers and the definitions. The popular wrong options came from half remembered ideas.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: Two questions were answered correctly by over 80 per cent of candidates.
Candidates did equally well on micro and macro questions.
mistakes: Many candidates did not understand when division of labour works best, and picked options about variety or skilled all rounders.
Candidates confused the link between price elasticity and the demand curve with unitary or inelastic cases.
Many used the full domestic output increase from a subsidy, ignoring that world supply already sets the price.
fix: Link division of labour to mass production, narrow tasks and predictable demand, not to flexible skills.
Remember that a horizontal demand curve means infinite elasticity, so a fall in demand cuts revenue by the same proportion.
Under world supply, start from the world price and recalculate domestic supply and imports before choosing.

questions.issue: Only about a third chose the right option. Many picked a market needing variety or custom goods.
questions.fix: Division of labour suits high volume, low variety output. Do not confuse specialised workers with multi skilled workers.

questions.issue: Fewer than one in five got it. Over half chose unitary elasticity, where revenue would not change.
questions.fix: Ask what happens to revenue. A same proportion fall means price is fixed, so the curve is horizontal.

questions.issue: Nearly three quarters chose the raw output gain and forgot that world supply sets the price.
questions.fix: Find domestic supply at the world price, compare it with demand, and read off the new import gap.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: Many candidates calculated a percentage change correctly and explained cross price elasticity for substitutes.
Most drew an accurate production possibility curve and explained scarcity and choice.
Many used AS/AD diagrams well to show how government spending and tax cuts affect demand.
mistakes: Some answers discussed price elasticity when the question asked for cross price elasticity, and scored nothing.
Diagrams were left incomplete, for example missing the original and new consumer surplus or full labels.
Many six mark answers ended without a judgement and just repeated earlier points.
Some candidates confused terms of trade with balance of trade and wrote about values, not prices.
The features of public goods were often blended, not defined separately as non rivalrous and non excludable.
fix: Check whether a percentage change is an increase or a decrease before you give the answer.
Draw the shift, label both equilibria and mark the surplus areas the question asks about.
End each evaluation with a clear judgement that uses your own analysis.
Write the terms of trade formula using export and import prices, and keep your explanation about prices.
Define each public good feature in its own sentence, with the reason after the word because.

questions.issue: Some candidates discussed the wrong elasticity. The good ones noted the positive sign for substitutes.
questions.fix: Name the correct measure, state the sign for substitutes and say what happens to demand.

questions.issue: Some diagrams missed the original and new surplus, and others analysed surplus without any supply shift.
questions.fix: Shift supply left first, then mark both surpluses and explain the smaller gap using elasticity.

questions.issue: Some strayed into the wider trade balance. Many good explanations had no final judgement.
questions.fix: Stay on import prices, mention elasticity and other sources, then give a short judgement.

questions.issue: Many gave little or no evaluation, though it carries a third of the marks.
questions.fix: Compare the free market with a mixed economy and reach a conclusion in the last paragraph.

questions.issue: Features were blended together without separate reasons, so knowledge marks were lost.
questions.fix: Define each feature separately and then apply them to the example, noting limits on access.

questions.issue: A significant number mixed it up with balance of trade and discussed values. That caps the mark at one.
questions.fix: Use export and import price changes and explain what one unit of exports can buy.

questions.issue: Labelling on AS/AD diagrams was often poor, which cost marks.
questions.fix: Label axes, curves and equilibrium points, then explain each shift in words.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Four questions were answered correctly by over 80 per cent of candidates.
Candidates did much better on micro questions than on macro ones.
mistakes: Many mixed up total revenue, total cost and profit on a marginal revenue diagram.
Many may have ignored the fixed part of the consumption function when finding the gap to full employment.
Candidates did not know that the IMF works on macro policy, not infrastructure lending.
fix: Remember that profit is maximised where MC equals MR and revenue is maximised where MR is zero.
Use the whole consumption function, including the fixed amount, then add investment before comparing.
Learn which jobs belong to the World Bank, the IMF or both.

questions.issue: Over three quarters chose answers including the extra cost area. They confused revenue with cost or profit.
questions.fix: Find each objective on the MR curve, then ask which area adds revenue and which adds cost.

questions.issue: The most popular options were gaps that may have come from dropping the fixed part of consumption.
questions.fix: Work out consumption at full employment income using the full formula, add investment, then compare.

questions.issue: The right answer was the least popular. Each other option was a shared role of both bodies.
questions.fix: Remember the IMF deals with macro policy and balance of payments, not infrastructure funding.

papers.title: A Level data response and essays
well: Many answers to the oligopoly essay were detailed, with an accurate kinked demand curve.
Most candidates did well on the part about how population change affects national output.
The essay on policies to reduce demand-pull inflation was handled very well, and about 90 per cent chose it.
Good answers used the Marshall-Lerner condition and J curve analysis to evaluate exchange rate policy.
mistakes: Candidates did not read key words and described population totals when the question was about population structure.
Most candidates wrote about a policy the government did not have, so that discussion earned nothing.
In the monopsony question, most drew a competitive labour market diagram instead, which led to wrong conclusions.
Some wrote about macro effects such as inflation in a question that was purely micro.
Evaluation of demand side policies was often one short sentence, which kept it at level 1.
fix: Underline the key words and check that every paragraph answers them.
Use only the policies the question names, and give a conclusion.
Draw the correct diagram for the market given, such as a monopsony diagram, and use it to trace the effect.
Keep a micro question micro. Leave out macro effects.
Develop each evaluation point over several sentences and separate short run effects from long run ones.

questions.issue: Weaker answers swapped in words like best or ideal. Others left out the given resources and technology condition.
questions.fix: Define it as the level with highest output per head, given resources and technology.

questions.issue: Most described totals instead of structure. Many said a falling growth rate meant falling population.
questions.fix: Write about birth rate, ageing and dependency, and read growth rate versus level carefully.

questions.issue: Over 90 per cent discussed a suggestion that was not government policy. Few gave a conclusion.
questions.fix: Cover only the policies the government actually used, and add a short conclusion.

questions.issue: Few moved past cursory evaluation, and game theory was rarely linked to collusion.
questions.fix: Link game theory to collusion, then evaluate using other goals such as break even or non price competition costs.

questions.issue: Most used a competitive labour diagram and some wrote about inflation, so many stayed at level 1.
questions.fix: Draw a monopsony diagram and use it to show wage and employment effects, then evaluate with elasticities.

questions.issue: Weaker answers drew micro diagrams instead of AS/AD, which blocked top marks.
questions.fix: Use a labelled AS/AD diagram and develop evaluation on both Keynesian and monetarist policies.

questions.issue: Many skipped the tariff diagram and rarely mentioned welfare loss. Retaliation was only briefly noted.
questions.fix: Draw a labelled tariff diagram, show welfare loss and develop retaliation as evaluation.

quote.text: linked directly to the written explanation

takeaways: Most wrong answers on multiple choice came from weak command of basic terms. I would drill definitions first, for example recession, derived demand, progressive tax and public finances.
Answer the exact question set. Candidates lost marks by writing about a nearby topic, such as inflation in general when the question was about a target rate.
Draw diagrams carefully, label every curve and point, and tie each one to your written explanation.
Evaluation needs reasons behind the judgement. Bare assertions and conclusions that only repeat earlier points fall short.
Never say a policy or effect always happens. Say when it works and when it does not.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: Most candidates got more than 20 questions right, a very good result overall.
Twenty questions were answered well.
mistakes: Wrong answers mostly came from not knowing basic terms.
Some candidates picked an option without checking if it was possible on the new production possibility curve.
Some confused complements with derived demand, and ignored the positive sign for income elasticity.
Some misread index numbers, and some used quantities, not prices, for the terms of trade.
Some candidates misjudged what a quota and a depreciation do to supply and prices.
fix: Learn the definition of each key term and test yourself on them.
Calculate before choosing when a question gives numbers, and check the option is possible.
Remember that complements are consumed together, while derived demand is demand for a good used to make another.
Read an index number series across all years and find the lowest year before answering.
Use the terms of trade formula with export and import prices, not quantities.

questions.issue: A common wrong answer was an output the new curve could not reach. It was not checked by calculation.
questions.fix: Work out the maximum from the hours given, then check it against the curve.

questions.issue: Some called a component good a complement, instead of seeing demand derived from the final product.
questions.fix: Ask whether the good is used to make another product. If so, think derived demand.

questions.issue: Some candidates ignored the positive sign, which means revenue falls when real GDP falls.
questions.fix: Apply the sign first. Positive income elasticity moves sales in the same direction as income.

questions.issue: A congested road was treated as non rivalrous, but congestion delays every user.
questions.fix: Test for rivalry by asking whether one user reduces the benefit for others.

questions.issue: Most did not know public finances means government spending and taxation.
questions.fix: Learn that tax and spending are fiscal policy, and interest rates and money supply are monetary.

questions.issue: Some mixed up the two. If the marginal rate is above the average rate, the tax is progressive.
questions.fix: Compare marginal and average rates. Marginal above average means progressive.

questions.issue: Some candidates compared quantities, but the formula uses export and import prices.
questions.fix: Write the formula first and check each option changes prices, not quantity.

questions.issue: Some missed that dearer imports raise costs of finished goods and raw materials.
questions.fix: Trace a weaker currency to higher import prices, higher costs and more inflation pressure.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: Strong answers used precise terms and had a logical structure.
Many diagrams were labelled clearly and used within the explanation.
Candidates who used the data in Section A pulled out numbers well for elasticity work.
Many put the maximum price below equilibrium and explained the shortage and non price rationing.
mistakes: Some candidates repeated the extract instead of answering every part of the question.
Definitions were incomplete. A few gave the price elasticity formula or no formula at all.
Some calculations used the percentage change in price when income was needed.
Maximum price diagrams sometimes sat above equilibrium or had no labels.
Some mixed up surplus with profit, or said producer surplus always falls.
fix: Read the whole question and plan which parts it asks for before writing.
Learn full definitions with formulae for the key syllabus terms.
Use the correct percentage change in each elasticity calculation and state what the sign means.
Place a maximum price below equilibrium, label both prices and show the shortage.
Check whether the surplus change came from a demand shift or a supply shift, then explain it.

questions.issue: Some described elasticity in general with no mention of income, and a few used the price formula.
questions.fix: State the formula as percentage change in quantity over percentage change in income.

questions.issue: Some copied the extract without linking it to information failure, or only discussed external effects.
questions.fix: Define a demerit good, explain imperfect information and say whether every product fits.

questions.issue: Some listed pros and cons without linking them to consumption, or just said another method was better.
questions.fix: Trace the tax to cost, price and demand, then weigh it against alternatives with reasons.

questions.issue: Some assumed unemployment would always rise and ignored workers moving to other sectors.
questions.fix: Consider labour mobility and jobs created in substitute industries, then judge the extent.

questions.issue: Diagrams put the price above equilibrium, and some answers said all consumers gain.
questions.fix: Draw the cap below equilibrium, show excess demand and say who gains and who loses.

questions.issue: Some listed points without linking them to income inequality or did not separate earned and state income.
questions.fix: Compare how each policy reaches households and discuss incentives and dependency.

questions.issue: Some diagrams missed a surplus, and some answers said producer surplus always falls.
questions.fix: Show both surpluses, and explain the effect by what caused the price fall and the elasticities.

questions.issue: Some described the tools without evaluating them, or repeated the same point for both.
questions.fix: Contrast price and quantity effects, certainty of protection, revenue and retaliation.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Most candidates got more than 20 questions right, a very good result overall.
Twenty questions were answered well.
mistakes: Wrong answers mostly came from not knowing subject terms.
Many did not know that oligopoly has little price competition.
Some forgot that a free market only counts private costs and benefits.
Some candidates mixed up the functions of the IMF and the World Bank.
Many did not know how the consumption function, autonomous and induced investment, or the recession definition work.
fix: Learn precise definitions and use them to remove wrong options.
Remember that a cartel finds it easier to fix prices when more firms belong.
Include the extra pay for existing workers when working out marginal cost.
Remember a recession means two consecutive quarters of negative growth.
Remember the IMF focuses on exchange rates and balance of payments help, while the World Bank lends.

questions.issue: Wrong options were equally popular because candidates missed the lack of price competition.
questions.fix: Link oligopoly to interdependence and non price competition.

questions.issue: Some chose an option that counted social costs, which needs government action.
questions.fix: In a free market, only private costs and benefits drive decisions.

questions.issue: A common wrong answer counted only the pay of new staff and ignored the raise for existing staff.
questions.fix: Add the higher wage for all current workers to the pay of the extra ones.

questions.issue: Most did not see that when marginal propensity to consume is below one, average propensity falls as income rises.
questions.fix: Compare the rise in consumption with the rise in income over the whole range.

questions.issue: Most were unsure of the terms. Induced investment responds to income, while the multiplier starts with autonomous investment.
questions.fix: Link the accelerator to changes in output and the multiplier to an initial autonomous injection.

questions.issue: Most did not use the technical definition of two quarters of negative growth.
questions.fix: Scan the diagram for runs of two negative quarters and count them.

questions.issue: Some included infant mortality, but the index uses life expectancy at birth.
questions.fix: Learn the three components of the index and what each measures.

questions.issue: Some thought the IMF lends finance to governments.
questions.fix: Keep the IMF for monetary cooperation, exchange rate stability and balance of payments help.

papers.title: A Level data response and essays
well: Candidates frequently drew relevant, accurately labelled diagrams.
Strong answers linked training to skills, productivity and pay, and weighed who should pay.
Good answers set out the costs and benefits of a zero inflation target, and used expectations in evaluation.
The best answers on trade and aid gave both equal weight, and used labelled diagrams.
mistakes: Answers did not stick to the specific question set.
Detailed comment was often replaced by general comment.
Weaker answers discussed general fiscal or monetary policy, not the specific policies named in the text.
In the market failure essay, weaker answers often wrote only about efficiency and missed the fairness focus.
Weaker answers wrote about types of inflation, and some about zero inflation, instead of a zero target rate.
fix: Pick out the key command word and key terms in the question and keep every paragraph tied to them.
When the data names specific policies, use those, then weigh up their advantages and disadvantages.
If the question says equitable, link efficiency to fairness and judge the outcome.
Build a diagram with both axes labelled and both curves, and show the shift with a two stage link.
Give both sides of a pair, such as trade and aid, equal depth, and make a judgement on their relative importance.

questions.issue: Limited answers could not pick out one of the two countries' fiscal responses from the bar chart.
questions.fix: Read the chart carefully for each item asked and match labels to bars.

questions.issue: Many did not see that stronger access to credit explained the bigger response.
questions.fix: Give two clear reasons, and think about borrowing ability.

questions.issue: Limited answers could not identify the shift of AD.
questions.fix: Label both axes and curves, shift AD the right way and add a two stage explanation.

questions.issue: Limited answers covered one sector only or did not develop factors enough to show the contrast.
questions.fix: Give two developed factors for each sector, then conclude on the difference.

questions.issue: Weak answers ignored firms and governments as payers and did not link skills to pay and productivity.
questions.fix: Consider other stakeholders, then judge the extent to which workers alone should pay.

questions.issue: Answers dwelt on efficiency and did not reach equity, which left evaluation thin.
questions.fix: After analysing efficiency, link it to fairness and conclude on the equity effect.

questions.issue: Limited answers described types of inflation, and some wrote about zero inflation, not the target itself.
questions.fix: Explain why central banks set targets, then discuss costs such as deflation and benefits such as lower menu costs.

questions.issue: Answers were descriptive, thin on aid, and ended with a summary, not a judgement.
questions.fix: Analyse each with a diagram where useful, give them equal weight and judge which matters more.

quote.text: evaluation requires some form of judgement and assessment

takeaways: Evaluation is a judgement, not a summary. Weigh both sides and say which wins and why. A summary of earlier points is not evaluation.
Read the command word and the key words before you write. Answers lost marks for writing about external causes when internal were asked, or minimum prices when maximum were asked.
When a diagram is asked for, draw the right one, label it fully and refer to it. If it is missing, you cannot get past Level 2.
In part (b) essays, use your concept to answer the question. Defining elasticity or public goods at length is not an answer.
Learn the pairs candidates keep confusing: terms of trade and balance of trade, public goods and merit goods, rivalry and excludability, budget and current account.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: One question was answered correctly by 95 per cent of candidates.
Candidates handled micro questions better than macro ones.
mistakes: Over four in five called a free state health service a public good.
Most could not use opportunity cost to find terms of trade that suit both countries.
Only 30 per cent found the right change in the injections and withdrawals model.
Most mixed up residency when working out how a worker's remittance affects the balance of payments.
fix: Test public goods for both non rivalry and non excludability before choosing.
Find each country's opportunity cost first, then pick terms lying between the two.
Remember equilibrium is withdrawals equal to injections, then pick the biggest imbalance.
Note which country the worker lives in, because that decides where the income is recorded.

questions.issue: Only 7 per cent were right. Most called state funded free health care a public good.
questions.fix: Check whether it is non rivalrous and non excludable. A free service can still be a private good.

questions.topic: Terms of trade from opportunity cost
questions.issue: Many chose a rate one country could already get without trade.
questions.fix: Calculate both opportunity costs and choose a rate strictly between them.

questions.issue: Many missed the equilibrium condition and which change causes the biggest gap.
questions.fix: Write withdrawals equal to injections, then pick the option with rising injections and falling withdrawals.

questions.issue: The most popular answer ignored where the worker is resident.
questions.fix: Find the country of residence first, then decide whether the flow is primary or secondary income.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: Candidates did well on a basic recall question about entrepreneurship and risk, with 95 per cent correct.
Four questions were answered correctly by 84 per cent or more.
Micro and macro questions were answered equally well.
mistakes: Over four in five called a free new road a public good.
Many chose a very inelastic supply as the full reason prices rise and ignored demand.
Many missed the word domestic and chose depreciation as a fall in the real value of a domestic currency.
Only a third read a table of real and nominal wages correctly when inflation is zero.
fix: A free road is not automatically a public good. Check whether scarce resources were used.
Give both a demand reason and a supply reason for a long run price rise.
Notice the key word in the stem. Inflation cuts what a currency buys at home, while depreciation is a fall against other currencies.
With zero inflation, real and nominal wages move together.

questions.issue: Only 8 per cent were right. Most said a free road is a public good.
questions.fix: Ask if it is non rivalrous and non excludable. If it used scarce resources, think private.

questions.issue: Most chose an answer about inelastic supply alone and left out rising demand.
questions.fix: Pick the option that explains both rising demand and inelastic supply.

questions.topic: Fall in value of a domestic currency
questions.issue: Nearly half chose depreciation, which is a fall against other currencies.
questions.fix: Read the word domestic and think about what lowers its real value, such as higher inflation.

questions.topic: Real and nominal wages with zero inflation
questions.issue: Only a third chose the only table consistent with zero inflation.
questions.fix: If prices do not change, real and nominal wages must move in the same direction.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: Three questions were answered correctly by 85 per cent or more.
Micro questions were answered better than macro ones.
mistakes: Many misread an opportunity cost table and picked the wrong statement.
Some placed trade in goods under primary income.
Some chose a policy that could still work when the question asked for the least effective supply-side policy.
Half thought higher government borrowing would widen the current account deficit.
fix: Calculate opportunity cost directly from the table before choosing.
Learn what is in primary income, and what is trade in goods.
Underline words like least or not, and sketch a quick diagram.
Link a bigger borrowing need to more bonds, lower bond prices and higher interest rates.

questions.issue: Only 36 per cent were right. The question asked for the statement that was not correct.
questions.fix: Divide what you give up by what you gain, and check the exact statement.

questions.topic: Primary income in balance of payments
questions.issue: Some chose trade in goods as primary income.
questions.fix: Primary income covers earnings like wages, interest and profits, not goods trade.

questions.issue: Just under half were right. Nearly three in ten chose an income tax cut, which can still help at full employment.
questions.fix: Spot the word least, then note that tax cuts can still lift productivity.

questions.issue: Half chose a larger current account deficit, which the information does not support.
questions.fix: Trace borrowing to bond supply, lower bond price and higher interest rates.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: Many candidates calculated real growth correctly by taking inflation from nominal growth.
Some compared two internal causes of growth and argued for capital investment.
Many explained why a currency appreciated through higher export demand.
Some gave balanced answers on maximum prices, including shortages, queues and illegal markets.
mistakes: Some wrote about external causes of growth when the question asked for internal ones.
A number wrote about the effects of appreciation in general, not terms of trade, and some misunderstood the term.
In the demand essay, many drew a movement along a curve, or an AD/AS diagram, instead of a demand shift.
Many answers on elasticity were general and not applied to the product in the question, and some brought in cross elasticity.
Some wrote about minimum prices instead of maximum prices.
fix: Pick the exact command word and key word, such as calculate, internal or assess, and answer only that.
Describe terms of trade as relative export and import prices, then judge whether all industries gain.
Draw a demand and supply diagram with a rightward demand shift and list causes such as income or tastes.
Define both elasticity measures briefly, then apply each to the firm and say which matters more.
For any assess question, give a balanced view and a judgement. One sided answers cannot be evaluated.

questions.issue: A few wrote external causes, and many ignored the data in the source.
questions.fix: Pick two internal causes, use figures, then judge which gives longer lasting growth.

questions.issue: Few explained that buyers need the currency to pay for exports.
questions.fix: Link higher export demand to higher demand for the currency in a short chain.

questions.issue: Some wrote generally and misunderstood terms of trade, and gave no evaluation of whether all industries gain.
questions.fix: Focus on relative prices of exports and imports, then say which industries gain or lose.

questions.issue: Many drew a movement, left out supply or drew AD/AS, and wrote about price instead of demand factors.
questions.fix: Shift demand right on a labelled demand and supply diagram, and compare short and long run price effects.

questions.issue: Answers were general, and many confused income elasticity.
questions.fix: Define both, apply each to a car maker and judge which matters more.

questions.issue: Some only summarised, and a few wrote about minimum prices.
questions.fix: Weigh gains and losses for consumers and producers, then conclude.

questions.issue: A number mixed up budget deficits with current account deficits, and links to fiscal aims were often missing.
questions.fix: Link deficit and surplus to expansion and contraction, and judge when each fits.

questions.issue: Many wrote all they knew about the theories and not their limits.
questions.fix: Name the limits such as two countries and no transport costs, then judge how much they matter.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: Most candidates calculated a percentage change correctly.
Most could give one reason why oil demand fell, and the best drew accurate diagrams for a supply problem.
Many wrote sound knowledge for public goods and spotted the free rider problem.
Analysis of why aggregate demand and aggregate supply increase was generally sound.
mistakes: Some subtracted figures and gave an absolute change, or forgot to show a fall.
Many could not link a demand fall to a price fall, and a leftward demand shift with no explanation was not enough.
Many treated a shortage of an input as a shift in the supply of the final good, without tracing the steps.
Answers on elasticity were vague, for example saying a small change causes a bigger change.
Many wrote about the causes of unemployment types, not their damaging effects.
fix: Calculate percentage change as change over the original, and say whether it is a rise or fall.
Explain price falls through the surplus that builds up and the cut needed to clear it.
Trace a shortage of an input to higher costs and then a higher price.
Define elasticity as a percentage change in quantity from a percentage change in price, or use a worked example.
Answer the question about effects, then compare them for seriousness and conclude.

questions.issue: Some gave an absolute difference or did not show a price fall.
questions.fix: Use change divided by the original value times 100 and show the minus sign.

questions.issue: Most scored one mark. They stated the fall without linking demand to price.
questions.fix: Say the surplus forces sellers to cut price, and explain the link in words, not just a diagram.

questions.issue: Many missed that the shortage was of an input, and asserted a left shift of final good supply.
questions.fix: Show the input market first, then costs, then the final price, then a way to fix the supply.

questions.issue: Many wrote on diversification in general and copied text instead of explaining.
questions.fix: Compare the two economies directly, explain each point and conclude.

questions.issue: Vague wording like a bigger change got no credit, and evaluation was asserted.
questions.fix: Use percentage change in quantity over percentage change in price, then add a reasoned judgement and a conclusion.

questions.topic: Public goods in a market economy
questions.issue: Some mixed up non excludable and non rivalry, and a few used roads or parks as examples.
questions.fix: Define each feature separately, pick a true example and link both to the free rider problem.

questions.topic: Terms of trade or balance of trade
questions.issue: Many described revenue and spending as if it were terms of trade, and defined balance of trade loosely.
questions.fix: Define terms of trade by prices, and balance of trade as export revenue minus import spending on goods.

questions.issue: Definitions just reworded the term, and diagrams had missing labels.
questions.fix: Define each with price level and its parts, then label price level, real output, AD and AS.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: Most candidates gained full marks on the first, straightforward part of the data response.
Many gave sound formulas for elasticity and explained recovery links between demand and jobs.
A number explained interest rate cuts well, including the effect on the exchange rate.
A number of strong answers analysed supply-side policies well.
mistakes: The most common slips were repeating the term in the question or not pointing to an official measure such as GDP.
Some could not justify an answer when the command word was justify.
Few linked recovery and demand to price stability, so marks rarely went above 2 out of 6.
Answers often spent a lot of time on how monetary policy works, and less on its drawbacks.
Answers on elasticity of supply often said a price rise gives a big change, not a percentage comparison.
fix: Define a term using an official measure, not by repeating the question.
When told to justify, give a reason from the data for your choice.
Cover both parts of a question, such as jobs and price stability.
Weigh the drawbacks of a policy, such as time lags, and compare it with alternatives.
Define elasticity as a percentage change in one variable from a percentage change in another.

questions.issue: A significant minority named the right answer but gave no reasoned justification.
questions.fix: Give a reason from the data. Follow the command word.

questions.issue: Most explained jobs but ignored price stability, so marks stayed low.
questions.fix: Use AD/AS to cover both jobs and prices, then judge.

questions.issue: Answers had a lot on how it works and little on drawbacks.
questions.fix: Cover drawbacks such as time lags, then compare with alternatives such as fiscal policy.

questions.issue: Answers were often imprecise, some confused it with PED, and few evaluated the effect on consumers and producers.
questions.fix: Show percentage change in supply from a price change, and explain why short run supply is less elastic.

questions.issue: Many defined measures at length and did not use them for the producer. That capped marks at Level 1.
questions.fix: State what each measure tells the producer, apply it to the product and compare.

questions.issue: Many confused public goods with merit goods and imprecisely defined the two features.
questions.fix: Decide using rivalry and excludability, then conclude that private goods can still be state run.

questions.topic: Supply-side policy and long term unemployment
questions.issue: Answers lacked focus on long term jobs and mixed short and long run effects.
questions.fix: Keep to long term unemployment and separate AD effects from AS effects.

questions.issue: Candidates confused domestic and external effects and considered negatives only.
questions.fix: Separate the home economy from trading patterns and exchange rates, and include positive effects.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Five questions were answered correctly by 70 per cent or more of candidates.
Those questions came from different parts of the syllabus.
mistakes: Answers were spread evenly across all four options on one question, which suggests guessing or a missed word like not.
Many believed any product with inelastic demand can support price discrimination.
Most did not know what a Measure of Economic Welfare adds to GDP.
fix: Underline the word not before you read the options.
Remember price discrimination needs more than inelastic demand, such as separate markets.
Learn that the welfare measure adjusts for environment, leisure and unpaid household work.

questions.topic: Cost curves between two output levels
questions.issue: Answers were evenly split. Candidates may have guessed or missed that the question asked for the false statement.
questions.fix: Test each statement true or false against fixed costs, long run average cost and diminishing returns.

questions.issue: Many chose any inelastic product as suitable, which is not enough.
questions.fix: Check that markets can be separated and that elasticity differs between groups.

questions.issue: Under a third were right. Candidates missed that the welfare measure adjusts GDP for several extra items.
questions.fix: Remember it adds leisure and unpaid household services and adjusts for environmental costs and benefits.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Five questions were answered correctly by 70 per cent or more of candidates.
mistakes: Many read total utility curves as if they were marginal utility curves.
Many misjudged what a merger of two large firms does to market structure.
Many wrongly thought a universal basic income does not cut the incentive to work.
fix: Check whether a utility curve is total or marginal before reading values.
Identify the structure before and after a merger by looking at market shares.
Remember a universal income has no test and no work requirement, so it can reduce work incentives.

questions.issue: About a third probably took the gap between total utility curves as marginal utility.
questions.fix: Find marginal utility from the change in total utility for one extra unit.

questions.issue: Under four in ten saw that the merger of the two large firms created a monopoly.
questions.fix: Add up the shares to see what the structure was, then what it is after the merger.

questions.issue: Many said it does not reduce the incentive to work, though everyone receives it regardless.
questions.fix: Ask what happens to the benefit when someone works. Here it stays the same.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Candidates scored a higher average than the year before.
Even among the four hardest questions, three were answered correctly by more than half.
mistakes: Many thought the question about improving productivity needed only one factor.
Almost half did not see that a cut in defence spending lowers national income.
Candidates split between two options on the IMF question, which asked about loan conditions.
On the policy aims question, many chose an option that did well on only one aim.
fix: Count all the options that raise productivity, such as education and capital allowances.
Treat lower government spending as a fall in demand and national income.
Remember IMF loans come with conditions such as reduced spending and trade liberalisation.
Score each option against every policy aim and pick the one that fits the most.

questions.issue: Many chose an answer with only one of the two helpful policies.
questions.fix: Check each option for effects on skills and on capital.

questions.issue: Almost half missed that less defence spending lowers national income.
questions.fix: Treat cuts in government spending as falls in demand.

questions.issue: Many chose the option that did best on jobs alone.
questions.fix: Score each option across growth, inflation, jobs and the balance of payments.

questions.issue: Candidates split between two options.
questions.fix: Link IMF loans to policy changes such as privatisation, trade liberalisation and lower public spending.

papers.title: A Level data response and essays
well: Some answers were well balanced and clearly structured, with relevant applications.
Most explained that low interest rates encourage borrowing and risk taking.
Better answers on the health care essay separated public from private ownership and named a merit good.
Good answers on monetary policy covered interest rates, money supply and exchange rates.
mistakes: Some did not direct their answer precisely at the question, such as discussing health care in general.
A number named causes of a trade deficit without explaining them. Listing four causes alone earned only 2 marks.
A number ignored the evidence given, and few judged whether it was enough.
On the interest rate part, evaluation that used the data was not done well.
A number did not spot the merger as horizontal integration, or gave no monopoly diagram.
fix: Pick the concepts the question points to, such as merit goods, positive externalities and allocative efficiency.
Give a short explanation for each cause, not a list.
Quote the evidence provided and comment on whether it is enough.
Draw a relevant labelled diagram even when one is not asked for, such as a monopoly diagram.
Even if an essay does not ask for evaluation, give it, because up to 6 marks are available.

questions.issue: Candidates needed to use the table and say the debt was over twice the size of output.
questions.fix: Refer directly to the table and the numbers.

questions.issue: A number ignored the evidence, few judged whether it was enough, and some missed the longer decline.
questions.fix: Use the figures given, say what they cannot show, and place the event in a longer trend.

questions.topic: Low interest rates and the economy
questions.issue: Evaluation using the data was weak.
questions.fix: Explain the effect with AD/AS and then use the data to weigh up its limits.

questions.topic: Health care as a merit good
questions.issue: Weaker answers were general and missed externalities and allocative efficiency.
questions.fix: Use a positive externality diagram and a developed evaluation at Level 2.

questions.issue: Some did not call it horizontal integration, or had no diagram.
questions.fix: Name the integration, draw a labelled monopoly diagram and argue both sides.

questions.issue: Effectiveness was thin, and other policies appeared rarely.
questions.fix: Link monetary policy to cyclical unemployment, then compare fiscal and supply-side policy.

questions.issue: Few described the traits of high and low income countries.
questions.fix: Cover both groups, link globalisation to free trade and conclude that it depends on factors.

papers.title: A Level data response and essays
well: Candidates generally knew the theory, and the best applied it to the question.
Most scored well on negative externality definition, labelled diagram and article examples.
Some well written answers on the consumer theory essay used labelled diagrams that split income and substitution effects.
Strong answers on the perfect competition essay defined productive and allocative efficiency and linked them to the stages.
mistakes: Some diagrams were poorly drawn or labelled, or were never referred to in the essay.
Some used learned answers that did not match the question.
About half did not know equity means fairness, and many forgot the poorer workers were the ones harmed.
Some wrote the consumer theory essay on marginal utility when indifference curves were asked for, limiting them to Level 1.
Weaker answers on perfect competition left out disequilibrium or did not cover types of efficiency.
fix: Draw neat diagrams, label them fully and use them in the written answer.
Answer the question set, not one you learned in advance.
Learn equity as fairness and use details from the article.
Use the method the question names, such as indifference curve analysis.
Cover disequilibrium and restoring equilibrium, and name both productive and allocative efficiency.

questions.issue: About half did not define equity as fairness, and many ignored that the poor workers lost out.
questions.fix: Define equity as fairness, then apply it to the groups affected.

questions.issue: Candidates who said both had merits missed the last mark.
questions.fix: Choose one alternative using article evidence and justify it.

questions.issue: Some knew the two features but could not apply them to transport.
questions.fix: Apply non rivalry and non excludability to the service, then conclude it is not a public good.

questions.issue: Some used marginal utility, which restricted them to Level 1.
questions.fix: Use indifference curves, split both effects and evaluate the assumptions about consumers.

questions.issue: Weaker answers ignored non equilibrium positions or one type of efficiency.
questions.fix: Show disequilibrium and equilibrium, apply both efficiencies, then compare with other market structures.

questions.issue: Some wrote about the standard of living rather than economic growth.
questions.fix: Define terms, analyse AD and capacity effects, and evaluate with exploitation.

questions.issue: Some ignored the standard of living, one measure, or wrote only on GDP.
questions.fix: Define the standard of living and compare both measures against it.

papers.title: A Level data response and essays
well: Most candidates explained actual growth as a rise in real GDP over time.
Most candidates gained at least two of three marks on equity versus equality.
Many candidates were well prepared on negative externalities and analysed them in depth.
Many candidates gave strong analysis on fiscal policy and a negative output gap.
