In 2(a), the majority gave survival or profit for ET and helping the community for Daycare.
Autocratic and democratic leadership were explained well by the majority in 4(a).
mistakes: Four topics were weakest: legal forms with and without incorporation, social enterprise objectives, the purpose of a cash flow forecast, and what marketing is for.
In 1(b), answers did not always compare the two options with each other, bringing in sole traders or public limited companies.
Most candidates struggled with 3(a), on why a cash flow forecast is needed before starting.
A minority of answers to 2(b) rested on opinions about staff or performance quality, not the appendix.
In 4(b), undeveloped lines about higher expense kept weaker answers in Level 1.
fix: Check the marks on each part, and write as the owners would think, not the staff.
Each section of an applied (a) question needs its own case detail. 1(a) was the generic one.
When a (b) question says use suitable calculations, the calculations must appear in your answer.
Follow a cost through: if refreshments cost more, prices may rise and ticket or refreshment sales may fall.

questions.issue: A few explained a quality using the same word, and some applied this generic question to ET.
questions.fix: Explain each quality in new words, focusing on the person rather than capital or a business plan.

questions.issue: Weaker answers took a private limited company to be part of the public sector, and some mirrored the legal identity point, which counts once.
questions.fix: Stronger answers developed how easy each form is to set up and how private its information stays. Finish by choosing one form and saying why the other is rejected.

questions.topic: Objectives for ET and for Daycare as a social enterprise
questions.issue: Weaker answers described how the objective would be met rather than why it was chosen, and a minority took ET to be running Daycare.
questions.fix: Explain why a new theatre would aim to survive, and why a social enterprise like Daycare puts the community first.

questions.topic: Option 1 or Option 2 for the opening performance
questions.issue: Weaker answers stopped at comparing raw appendix data, such as Option 2's higher forecast revenue, and some called Option 1 a loss without the number.
questions.fix: Calculate both: Option 1 loses $210 and Option 2 makes $260 per performance, then judge.

questions.topic: Reasons to prepare a cash flow forecast before starting
questions.issue: Confusing cash flow with profit was the most common error, and most who found correct reasons did not apply them to the theatre.
questions.fix: Reasons such as planning ahead and avoiding a liquidity problem count. Link each to the theatre before it opens, and remember it looks ahead, not back.

questions.issue: Weaker answers restated the roles, so the three parts overlapped, and a small minority described methods such as primary research instead of why each role matters.
questions.fix: Show what each role does for ET's audience in a low income area, then pick one and say why.

questions.issue: Some explained a style under the wrong heading, such as autocratic under democratic, and generic answers lost the application marks.
questions.fix: Match each explanation to its named style, and tie it to how Zane and Zaara would manage ET's 24 part-time employees.

questions.topic: Biggest effect of three ethical issues
questions.issue: A small number read fair wages as identical pay for everyone, and argued the best qualified staff would lose motivation.
questions.fix: Weigh each issue's gain against its cost, such as cheaper local transport but possibly lower quality costumes.

papers.title: Case study
well: Candidates had been well prepared, and results were broadly comparable with previous years.
1(a) on reasons to become a multinational was accessible for the majority.
The majority gave rewardable points in 1(b), and it was well applied using Appendix 1.
The majority gave an opportunity and a threat of ecommerce in 4(a), with good application.
mistakes: The weakest areas were the roles of directors and managers, and the problems a business faces as it expands.
Points on promotion and communication methods were often listed without saying why they mattered.
In 2(a) and 2(b), application was often missing.
Weaker answers to 3(b) gave mirror arguments or used the same training point for both options.
Some knew the 4(b) calculations but could not explain why the figures changed.
fix: Spread your case details: one new reference per section of an (a) question.
Say why each point is an advantage or a disadvantage for RR.
Justify the chosen option and say why the others are less suitable, without repeating earlier points.
Think about the consequences now and later before you recommend.

questions.topic: Reasons to become a multinational company
questions.issue: Several explained how a business becomes multinational rather than why.
questions.fix: Give reasons such as producing where costs are lower or nearer the market.

questions.issue: Many did not explain why their points helped or hurt the business.
questions.fix: Use the Appendix 1 figures, explain each method's effect on RR, then justify one choice.

questions.issue: Some gave two explanations of one point, and vague lines such as it is expensive scored little.
questions.fix: Pick two problems, such as poor communication, and apply both to the rug business.

questions.issue: Lists such as cheaper or quicker kept answers at Level 1.
questions.fix: Explain why each feature helps or hinders RR's 30 production employees.

questions.topic: Responsibilities of directors, managers, supervisors and employees
questions.issue: Many did not seem to know what directors and managers are responsible for, and weaker answers just described the organisational chart.
questions.fix: State what each level is responsible for, such as supervisors making sure work is done correctly.

questions.issue: Weaker answers used mirror points on motivation, or the same training cost for both options.
questions.fix: Give each option its own effects on productivity, then justify your pick and say why the other one loses.

questions.issue: Many needed more detail on why each was an opportunity or a threat.
questions.fix: Develop each, for example customers abroad cannot feel a rug before buying, so some may not buy.

questions.topic: Concern about financial performance, with calculations
questions.issue: Weaker answers only compared figures or thought a rise in cost of sales was good.
questions.fix: Show the gross profit margin falling from 60 to 50 per cent while the profit margin rose from 20 to 25 per cent, then explain why.

quote.text: if output doubled then everything else would double

takeaways: Learn full definitions. On Paper 12, inflation needed a rise in prices plus the time element for both marks, and many left out time.
Give each point its own detail from the stem or case, and develop your second point with fresh analysis rather than the first one's.
In each part (e) on Paper 12, give a decision, the reason behind it and why it beats the other option. A summary of earlier points earns nothing extra.
Revise the whole syllabus. On Paper 12, some candidates did not know sampling or legal controls over marketing, and most struggled with both questions.
On Paper 22, read the appendix data carefully and question it. Do not assume figures simply double when output doubles.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Candidates knew the concepts well overall, and the opening (a) and (b) parts of each question went well for most.
Ways technology can change production methods in 1(b) were well answered by most.
Most gave correct responsibilities of supervisors in 3(a), and methods of written communication in 3(b) were well answered.
Most knew sources of finance in 3(e) and gained the knowledge marks.
Defining quality control in 4(b) was well answered by most.
mistakes: Many definitions lacked precision or range, which held back marks in parts (a) and (b).
Some answered part (c) with analysis and part (e) with application, and neither skill is marked there.
Some were not familiar with sampling or with legal controls over marketing.
Of those who tried to evaluate, many gave a decision with no reasoned support.
Repeating a point in different words, as in 2(c) and 3(c), only counted once.
fix: Match your answer to the skills marked: part (c) wants knowledge, sometimes with application, while part (e) wants knowledge, analysis and evaluation.
For parts (c) and (d), pick details from the stem, and never the same one twice. 2(c) tested knowledge only.
Explain why your chosen option is better than the other one you discussed, rather than restating your points.
Do not define the term in a part (e) answer. Go straight to the points the question asks for.

questions.issue: Most knew prices rise, but only the strongest gave a full definition. Many left out time, explaining causes was a common mistake, and others wrote cost or one product instead of general prices.
questions.fix: Say it is a general rise in prices across the economy over a period of time.

questions.topic: Whether manufacturers always benefit from import tariffs
questions.issue: Challenging for most. Some wrote about whether to import at all, some mixed tariffs up with quotas, and evaluation was rare.
questions.fix: Weigh dearer imported rivals against dearer imported raw materials, then say what the answer depends on.

questions.issue: A common mistake was working out the current ratio instead. A slip in the last step could still earn the method mark.
questions.fix: Take inventory away from current assets, divide by current liabilities and show the working. The answer was 0.5.

questions.issue: A common mistake was listing types of inventory instead of reasons, and some gave the same reason twice in other words.
questions.fix: Give four separate reasons, such as keeping production going, bulk buying discounts and seasonal demand.

questions.topic: Why employees and suppliers are interested in financial statements
questions.issue: Few backed their points with the case data. Some just reused the question's wording, and a common misconception was that profit pays wages or suppliers.
questions.fix: Quote figures from Table 2.1, such as the loss of $10 000 or the fall in cash, and say what each group would decide.

questions.topic: Advantage and disadvantage of autocratic leadership
questions.issue: Most knew the disadvantages well, but many struggled with the advantage, saying who decides or just that it is quicker.
questions.fix: Say decisions are quicker because no one else is consulted, so AH can respond to chances such as the takeover sooner.

questions.topic: Ways legal controls affect marketing strategy
questions.issue: Poorly answered. Most could not give two different ways, and some wrote about employment or environmental law.
questions.fix: Give effects such as no misleading claims in adverts or changes to what the packaging says.

questions.topic: Reasons for using sampling in market research
questions.issue: Most found sampling challenging. A common misconception was that it is a separate research method, and application was rare.
questions.fix: Say it is cheaper and quicker than researching the whole market, and link each reason to Viktor's new photography business.

questions.topic: Ways a service business could motivate employees
questions.issue: Some said a method motivates without explaining how, a common mistake was choosing piece-rate pay, which does not suit services, and many summarised instead of evaluating.
questions.fix: Pick two methods that fit a service business, develop each, then justify which works better. No application is needed.

papers.title: Case study
well: The majority had been well prepared, and high scoring scripts were common.
1(a) on flow production was well answered.
The majority identified two problems of growth in 2(a).
3(a) went well, with many naming four legal controls that protect employees.
3(b) was generally well answered, with a good understanding of the two training methods.
mistakes: Some found external costs and benefits harder than other topics.
In 1(a), some listed several advantages and disadvantages instead of developing one of each.
In 2(b), a number of answers misread the appendix, for example thinking Location A needed no new factory.
In 2(b), development often stopped at simple impacts such as costs going up or down.
4(b) was the most challenging question, and only a few strong answers reached a conclusion on profit.
fix: Check the marks and the number of points asked for. Extra advantages beyond one earn nothing.
Take each point further. Say what happens to RW and why that matters.
Tie the recommendation to RW and give the reasons for rejecting the other choices.
To move beyond Level 1, think through the short-term and long-term consequences of each option.

questions.topic: Advantage and disadvantage of flow production
questions.issue: Weaker answers lacked development or listed several points, and both points needed applying for full marks.
questions.fix: Develop one advantage, such as lower unit costs, and one disadvantage, such as a breakdown halting output, each tied to the paint.

questions.topic: Tastes, incomes or rivals' prices: the biggest effect on RW's revenue
questions.issue: Higher incomes were assumed to lift sales without always saying why, and answers on tastes sometimes forgot that RW supplies the furniture makers.
questions.fix: Trace each change through to RW's paint sales, then justify which change matters most and why the others matter less.

questions.issue: Full marks needed three linked points for each problem as well as application.
questions.fix: State the problem, explain why it arises, then give its effect on RW, such as higher unit costs.

questions.topic: Choice of location for the new factory
questions.issue: A number of answers misread the data, for example treating each site as a new market or the port as a place to dump waste.
questions.fix: Ask how much each feature matters to RW and why, then reject the other two sites with reasons.

questions.issue: Weaker answers gave benefits to employers or to trade union members, and some applied this generic question to RW.
questions.fix: Name each law, then explain how it helps the worker. No application is needed here.

questions.issue: Some listed points without explaining them, some stayed theoretical, and some wrote mirror answers on cost.
questions.fix: Explain effects on cost, efficiency or labour turnover for RW, then justify your choice of method.

questions.issue: Weaker answers wrote about costs and benefits to the business in general, such as more sales.
questions.fix: Give effects on others, such as river pollution or local jobs, each linked to a case detail.

questions.topic: Whether forecast revenue, costs and profit are accurate
questions.issue: Many simply assumed every figure would double along with output. Some mixed up cost of sales with revenue, or took expenses to mean buying raw materials.
questions.fix: Question each figure, for example a new factory may need more than a year to sell its full output, then judge the profit.

quote.text: It is not about repeating the data

takeaways: Count what the question asks for. On Paper 12 a significant number gave several ways when one was asked for, or only one factor when two were asked for.
Half the marks on the 12 mark questions in Papers 12 and 22 are for evaluation. I would plan a clear, justified judgement before you start writing the analysis.
Use the business in the question. A new restaurant, a fruit farm or a wedding gift maker each needs its own details in your answer, or the application marks go.
On Paper 32, show every step of a calculation. The promotion question had no method marks, and many ARR answers stopped at three marks because the average investment was missing.
On Paper 42, do not retell the timeline. Pick the two or three most important parts of the strategy, analyse them together and reach a judgement on the question.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: The short Section A definitions were answered with confidence by most, who showed a sound grasp of the concepts.
Most defined opportunity cost correctly as the next best option given up.
Induction training was generally well understood, and many linked it to new employees.
Candidates generally gave sound extension strategies, such as new advertising or packaging, and applied them well.
On the cash flow forecasting essay, most candidates understood the idea and gained both knowledge marks.
mistakes: A significant number did not follow the instruction on Questions 4, 5(a) and 6(a): several ways where one was wanted, or only one factor where two were wanted.
Many showed little evaluation on 5(b) and 6(b), even after sound analysis.
Less successful answers to 1(b) often listed several qualities, and in 3(b) a common problem was two or three benefits with too little explanation.
Some answers to 2(b) wrote about developing new products instead of extending the life of the existing one.
On the new restaurant essay, many did not explain what is specific to a restaurant, which shut them out of the application marks and the top evaluation level.
fix: Underline the number in the question. One way means one way; two factors means two, each analysed.
Questions 4, 5(a) and 6(a) need analysis only. Save judgement for the 12 mark (b) parts, where it carries 6 marks.
For an explain one question, choose one point and develop it in the business setting.
Bring in features of the business named in the essay, such as the cost of ingredients or skilled chefs in a restaurant.
End every 12 mark answer with a judgement tied to that business, not a general one.

questions.issue: Most gave the next best option given up, but few referred directly to the costs incurred or benefits involved in making the choice.
questions.fix: The scheme's clear definition is the benefits lost or costs incurred when choosing between options, so name what is given up.

questions.topic: Quality an entrepreneur needs for success
questions.issue: Weaker answers listed several qualities, and some picked a quality that is not really an entrepreneurial one.
questions.fix: Pick one quality such as risk taking or innovation and apply it to someone starting a business.

questions.topic: Extending the life of a product
questions.issue: Some explained more than one strategy, and some wrote about new products instead.
questions.fix: Explain one extension strategy for the existing product and show how it attracts customers.

questions.issue: A common problem was two or three benefits, each with too little explanation.
questions.fix: Take one benefit, such as better skills, and follow it to fewer errors or more efficient work.

questions.issue: Some gave more than one way, and their analysis stayed limited.
questions.fix: Start with productivity as output compared with inputs, then follow one way, such as training, through to more output or less waste.

questions.topic: Cash flow forecasting and a new restaurant
questions.issue: Many gave no restaurant details, and weaker answers had very little evaluative comment.
questions.fix: Show why cash matters to a new restaurant, weigh it against other factors such as marketing or customer experience, then judge.

questions.issue: Candidates seemed less sure here. Weaker answers covered only one change or one effect, and some drifted into stakeholders in general.
questions.fix: Name a change, such as survival to growth, and analyse two effects on shareholders, such as dividends or selling shares.

questions.topic: Fast growth and niche cake businesses failing
questions.issue: Top evaluation marks went only to judgements tied to fast growth and failure in a niche cake business.
questions.fix: Give other causes of failure, such as poor cash control or competition, and judge whether growth is really the main one.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: Candidates engaged well with both cases, and most finished the paper.
Most named a correct content theory of motivation in 1(a)(i).
The pay calculation in 1(b)(i) was reasonably well done, and many worked out both payment systems.
Sole trader was well understood, and most gained the basic knowledge marks.
Candidates did well on 2(c) and applied it easily, and most gave just one advantage and one disadvantage.
Many saw that 2(d) asked about factors affecting the choice of finance, not which source to pick.
mistakes: In 2(b)(ii) the Table 2.1 data and the 2(b)(i) answer were rarely used to apply the advantage to Tomas.
Many spent too long on analysis in the 12 mark questions, often over half the answer, though only two marks were for analysis.
Some ignored the context, which always limits the mark.
Some missed the 50 per cent mark up in 2(b)(i) because they did not use the other information.
Some spent a long time in 2(d) judging which source of finance suits Tomas, which earned nothing.
fix: For identify questions, a single word or name is enough. No sentence is needed.
In explain questions, keep any definition short and spend the time applying it, to the named business where there is one.
In 12 mark questions, one chain of analysis covers the analysis marks. Aim to give about half the answer to evaluation.
Use your own calculation from part (b)(i) as application in part (b)(ii).
Read every instruction in a calculation, including any extra information outside the table.

questions.issue: Some saw it only as moving raw materials in, not the whole chain out to customers.
questions.fix: Show more than one part of the chain, such as raw materials coming in and finished goods going out to buyers.

questions.topic: Piece rate and time based pay
questions.issue: Occasionally candidates forgot to find the difference between the two.
questions.fix: Piece rate: 5 x 2 = 10, 2 x 1.50 = 3, 4 x 3 = 12, total $25. Time based: 8 x 4.50 = $36. Difference: 36 minus 25 = $11.

questions.topic: Advantage to FF of time based pay
questions.issue: Most knew plenty about time based pay but did not apply it to FF.
questions.fix: Use your figures from 1(b)(i) or other details of FF to show what the change means for the farm.

questions.topic: Two non-financial motivators for fruit pickers
questions.issue: The report notes that anything with a financial benefit to staff, such as fringe benefits, does not count as non-financial.
questions.fix: Choose motivators the case points to, such as better induction training, and link them to productivity, costs and profit.

questions.topic: Impact on stakeholders of more sustainable operations
questions.issue: Knowledge of sustainability showed gaps. The question was about operations that can keep producing in future, and the environment should not have been the focus.
questions.fix: Treat sustainable operations as producing now without harming future production, and give about half the answer to evaluation.

questions.issue: Some wrote a paragraph where one word would do.
questions.fix: Write land, labour, capital or enterprise and move on.

questions.issue: Some left out the mark up.
questions.fix: Total cost: 250 x 1.20 = $300, plus $150 fixed costs = $450. Price: 450 x 1.5 = $675.

questions.topic: Advantage of cost-based pricing for Tomas
questions.issue: The data in Table 2.1 and the 2(b)(i) answer were rarely used.
questions.fix: Give an advantage, not a definition, and support it with Tomas's own figures.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: There were many excellent scripts that kept a clear focus on the questions.
Most saw that Questions 1 and 2 asked for analysis only, and built chains of reasoning in context.
Candidates frequently scored highly on Questions 1 and 2.
Many knew the right formula for price elasticity of demand, so earned at least one mark.
Candidates understood enterprise resource planning well, as software for planning how resources are bought and used.
mistakes: Marks were lower on 3(c), 4(b) and 5, mainly because evaluation was not developed.
Answers that tried to cover many points tended to have weaker evaluation and lower marks.
In 3(b) errors in the percentage changes were frequent, the most common error was missing that the answer is negative, and a considerable number inverted the formula.
In 4(a) many missed the average investment.
On Question 5 many simply repeated the ratios, and some read rises as falls because the newest year sat on the left.
fix: Read the case carefully and plan before you write.
Keep to a few key points and develop the evaluation of each.
Use the original figure as the base for every percentage change.
Show each stage of a calculation so method marks can be given.
Make judgements through the 12 mark answers and ground them in the business.

questions.topic: Impact of two planned legal changes on FWB
questions.issue: No marks went to simply restating the changes from the case.
questions.fix: Take one change, such as a higher minimum wage, and follow it: three staff per van paid more, so higher costs and lower profit.

questions.topic: Benefits to FWB of delegating to van managers
questions.issue: Some added disadvantages or judged the extent, and a few applied only one of the two benefits to FWB.
questions.fix: Analyse two benefits only, each in context, for example motivation helping to keep experienced managers.

questions.issue: Less than half got the right answer, and there were no method marks.
questions.fix: Multiply the change in promotion by the elasticity: 0.8 x 20 = 16 per cent.

questions.topic: Price elasticity of demand for coffee
questions.issue: Common errors were the wrong base, missing the negative sign and an inverted formula.
questions.fix: Change in quantity: minus 10 / 180 x 100 = minus 5.56 per cent. Change in price: 0.30 / 2.00 x 100 = 15 per cent. PED = minus 5.56 / 15 = minus 0.37 (or minus 0.4).

questions.topic: Usefulness of elasticity for a new marketing mix
questions.issue: Many said inelastic promotional demand made more promotion pointless, ignoring that a small spend could bring a much larger rise in revenue.
questions.fix: Use your 3(a) or 3(b) figure, then weigh it against FWB's objectives and how competitors may react.

questions.issue: Many divided by the full cost instead of the average investment and got 7.69 per cent for three marks.
questions.fix: Total savings 900 000 minus cost 650 000 = 250 000. Divide by 5 years = 50 000. Then 50 000 / 325 000 x 100 = 15.38 per cent.

questions.topic: Whether FWB should invest in ERP
questions.issue: Application was often limited to quoting the ARR.
questions.fix: Compare the ARR with FWB's ROCE, link ERP to FWB's waste problem and just in time stock control, and judge whether finance is available given the gearing.

questions.topic: Usefulness of ratio analysis to directors
questions.issue: This was the hardest question. Stating that gearing rose or the current ratio stayed the same earned nothing without understanding.
questions.fix: Explain what a ratio means for a decision, such as gearing and how to fund expansion abroad, then weigh it against other information.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: Strong candidates chose the most important data to reach a justified judgement on the marketing strategy.
The strongest answers analysed two or three key parts of the strategy together as one plan.
Many compared Porter's five forces with other approaches, which the report calls reasonable while Porter stays central.
mistakes: Many restated the timeline and appendices in other words, which gave long answers with no marks.
Answers that treated each decision separately could only analyse each one briefly.
Many left their evaluation to a small final paragraph, although evaluation is 40 per cent of the marks on Question 1.
A large proportion never judged how successful the marketing strategy was.
On Question 2, occasionally candidates covered Porter briefly and spent most of the answer on other approaches, or tried to cover too many of them.
fix: Treat the four Ps as one plan and analyse how they work together.
Make each point say whether it shows success, failure or depends on something.
Build evaluation from the start of the answer, not only at the end.
Neither verdict is penalised as long as it is justified, so commit to one.
On a technique question, analyse the technique itself and use the case figures as context.

questions.topic: Success of S2U's marketing strategy, 2016 to 2022
questions.issue: Many retold the data and analysed decisions one by one. A large proportion gave no judgement on success.
questions.fix: Combine the main parts of the marketing mix into one argument, judge success throughout, and finish with a clear verdict.

questions.topic: Usefulness of Porter's five forces for S2U
questions.issue: Occasionally Porter was covered thinly before a long look at other approaches, and many restated facts such as low barriers to entry.
questions.fix: Weigh the technique's usefulness for S2U; if you compare, one other approach is enough. Then advise Ruhi.

quote.text: abbreviating headings which is always unacceptable in financial statements

takeaways: Basic double entry was the weak spot on Paper 22. Practise ledger accounts and journal entries until you can say both sides without thinking, and always carry the balance down.
Write headings such as gross profit and cost of sales in full in every statement. Short forms cost marks.
When an advice question names two options, discuss both and back your decision with reasons. On Paper 32 Question 1(e), say yes or no and support it with the figures the question asks for.
Check each ratio formula against what goes in it: on Paper 32 many left the dividend out of earnings, put the overdraft into gearing or forgot finance costs in ROCE.
On multiple choice, work out whose books you are in and test bank answers with a quick reconciliation. On Paper 12 Question 2, the most popular wrong answer was the exact reverse of the key.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Question 1 was straightforward, and 74 per cent chose the key.
The mean score was 15 out of 30, and 52 per cent of candidates scored 15 or more.
The report says no question was very difficult.
mistakes: On Question 2, many chose the option that showed the customer account the wrong way round.
On Question 8, over a third chose A, the same share as chose the key.
On Question 10, answers were spread almost evenly across all four options.
On Question 11, just over a third chose an option that includes errors of commission, which a control account cannot find.
On Question 15, many left trade discounts received out of the items that affect gross profit.
fix: Before you answer, decide whose books the question is about: the customer's or the supplier's.
For suspense account corrections, think about the other side of each correcting entry.
Test a bank answer with a quick bank reconciliation if time allows.
Remember what a control account cannot reveal, such as a posting to the wrong customer or supplier.
Trade discount received lowers the cost of purchases, so it changes gross profit.

questions.topic: Customer account in the supplier's books
questions.issue: Many chose C, which puts the balance b/d on the credit side and the bank and discount allowed on the debit side.
questions.fix: A credit customer starts as a debit balance in the supplier's books. The key is A: balance b/d 600 on the debit side, bank 588 and discount allowed 12 on the credit side.

questions.topic: Advantage of keeping complete double entry records
questions.issue: Some chose C, which was about finding mistakes on the bank statement. That check does not need complete double entry records.
questions.fix: The key is A: with full double entry, account balances are available throughout the year.

questions.topic: Debit entry to the suspense account
questions.issue: Over a third chose A, 47 340. The report's own working ends at 97 560, but the key is C.
questions.fix: Item 1 does not involve suspense. Taking the 48 300 off the debit side and putting it on the credit side needs a debit of 2 x 48 300 = 96 600. The overcast provision needs a credit to suspense of 960. Net debit: 95 640, option C.

questions.issue: Candidates found it hard, and the four options were chosen in almost equal numbers.
questions.fix: Start from 12 697, add the uncleared 2 400 and take off the 450 standing order: 14 647. Add the 540 overstated cheque and the 642 interest: 15 829, option D.

questions.topic: Advantages of a purchases ledger control account
questions.issue: Just over a third picked C, the option that adds detecting errors of commission.
questions.fix: A control account cannot detect an item posted to the wrong supplier. The key is D: statements 3 and 4 only, checking staff honesty and finding the total owed quickly.

questions.topic: Items affecting a sole trader's gross profit
questions.issue: Only a third chose the key, and many chose B, carriage inwards only. The report suggests candidates may have mixed up trade and settlement discounts.
questions.fix: The key is A: carriage inwards and trade discounts received both change the cost of purchases.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: The examiners saw some excellent work from well prepared candidates.
Layout and presentation of financial statements keep improving, and more candidates show tidy workings.
Most candidates did the appropriation account in 1(b) very well, and most gave a very good reason for interest on drawings in 1(d).
Most calculated all three ratios in 3(a) correctly, and the break-even point in 4(c) was generally well answered.
Most defined capital expenditure well, and the capital expenditure total in 2(e)(i) was generally well answered.
mistakes: Basic double entry skills seemed weak, for example in the interest on drawings entry and the kitchen equipment account.
Many written answers were too thin. A single word or a short phrase is rarely enough.
Most found 1(c) very challenging, and many did not adjust for the change in profit without an agreement.
In 1(f), several discussed only one of the two options, and the advice often lacked justification.
The depreciation journal in 2(c) was very poorly answered, with wrong charges and workings that lacked structure.
In 3(c), very few correct ways to improve the acid test ratio were given, and stepped costs and marginal costing benefits caused trouble in 4(a) and 4(b).
fix: Show clear workings in every calculation, since valid workings always earn marks.
Write labels in full and learn the accepted layouts, including the marginal costing statement.
Round trade receivables and trade payables days up to the next whole day, and give other ratios to the decimal places asked for.
The report says a break-even point in units is always rounded up to a whole unit.
In an advice question with two options, discuss both, then give a decision with reasons.

questions.topic: Partnership statement of profit or loss
questions.issue: Very few were fully correct. The allowance for irrecoverable debts and the loan interest were the most common errors, and some still shortened headings.
questions.fix: Show the unwanted allowance of 380 as income, add the two accrued months of loan interest to the 750 paid (900 in all), and write every heading in full.

questions.topic: Current account without a partnership agreement
questions.issue: Many had little idea how to start, and many did not adjust for the change in profit.
questions.fix: Redo Nibras's current account both ways and compare the closing balances. Without the agreement there is no interest on capital or salary, Raif's loan interest falls to 5 per cent (450), so profit becomes 10 380, shared equally (5 190 for Nibras).

questions.topic: Double entry for interest on drawings
questions.issue: Answers were variable, and many sent the entries through the drawings account or the cash or bank account.
questions.fix: Debit the partners' current accounts and credit the appropriation account.

questions.issue: Common errors were wrong details and not carrying the closing balance down.
questions.fix: Debit balance b/d 3 450 and cash 1 680. Credit depreciation to the statement of profit or loss 1 180 and balance c/d 3 950, then bring the 3 950 down.

questions.issue: Many scored nothing, mostly from a wrong charge and unstructured workings.
questions.fix: Old vehicle net book value 24 000 minus 10 500 = 13 500. New vehicle cost 22 500 plus 13 500 = 36 000. Depreciation 25% x 36 000 = 9 000. Debit statement of profit or loss, credit provision for depreciation.

questions.issue: Many struggled to pick out the capital receipts.
questions.fix: Add the bank loan 25 000, the extra capital 40 000 and the furniture disposal 2 800: 67 800.

questions.topic: Ways to improve the acid test ratio
questions.issue: Very few correct answers. Many suggested selling more at a higher price, more credit sales or cutting trade payables.
questions.fix: The scheme credits ideas such as reducing cash drawings, borrowing long term, putting in more capital or selling non-current assets.

questions.issue: Few correct responses. Many wrote that it helps decision-making without saying short term.
questions.fix: Scheme points include avoiding arbitrary apportionment of fixed costs, avoiding under or over absorption, and help with short term decisions.

papers.title: Financial accounting
well: Questions 1 and 2 were generally satisfactory and better than Question 3.
Many produced a fully correct provision for unrealised profit account.
The manufacturing account and the statement of profit or loss were prepared to a high standard.
Most gave advice in 1(e) with two points to justify it, and many worked out the dividend yield correctly.
Most named the correct accounting standard in both parts of 3(a).
mistakes: Most knew what factory profit is, but few explained two reasons for using it.
Ratio work slipped: the dividend was not added to retained earnings, the overdraft went into gearing, and few added finance costs for ROCE.
In 2(b)(i), very few gave more than two valid points on the price earnings ratio, and in 2(c) very few developed their points enough to pass three of the five marks.
In 3(b), some took both the proposed dividend and the revaluation loss off the draft figure.
The adjusted statement of financial position was weaker, with very few correct property, plant and equipment figures.
In 3(d), very few could state three responsibilities of an external auditor.
fix: When asked to explain two reasons, give each reason and then say why it matters.
Support advice with calculations whenever the question asks for them.
Build each ratio from its parts, checking what belongs in the numerator and the denominator.
In analysis questions, compare with the industry average and say what the difference means.
Learn at least three external auditor responsibilities.

questions.issue: Few gave an acceptable explanation of two reasons.
questions.fix: Scheme reasons include comparing with the price of buying from outside suppliers, and treating manufacturing as a profit centre so costs are controlled.

questions.issue: Errors included the factory overheads adjustment and the treatment of work in progress.
questions.fix: Move the 3 000 repair wages from direct labour into overheads and the 1 000 office equipment depreciation out to administration (85 000 + 3 000 minus 1 000 = 87 000), then add the 960 fall in work in progress.

questions.topic: Whether to accept a sales order
questions.issue: Full marks were rare because the supporting calculations were often left out.
questions.fix: The scheme uses an effective margin of 443 000 / 936 000 = 47.33%, then 40 000 x 47.33% minus 9 500 = 9 432 extra profit.

questions.issue: Profit missed the dividend, the overdraft went into gearing, and finance costs were left out of ROCE.
Very few gave more than two valid points.
questions.fix: Compare 18.61 with the industry 16, then say what it shows about investor confidence and expected growth.

questions.issue: Marks were often lost on the impairment figure and an unclear recoverable amount.
questions.fix: Name IAS 36. Recoverable amount is the higher of 22 700 (24 500 minus 1 800) and value in use 23 200. Impairment 27 000 minus 23 200 = 3 800, charged to profit or loss.

questions.issue: Depreciation and repair adjustments were mishandled, and some deducted the proposed dividend and revaluation loss.
questions.fix: The scheme adds back the proposed dividend of 20 000 and the revaluation loss of 35 000. The loss comes off the revaluation reserve instead (60 000 minus 35 000 = 25 000).

questions.issue: Very few reached the correct property, plant and equipment figure, and relatively few completed current assets and liabilities correctly.
questions.fix: Carry each adjustment from 3(a) and 3(b) into the statement, including the impairment and the new provision.

papers.title: Cost and management accounting
well: Question 2 was answered better than Question 1.
Nearly all set the cash budget out acceptably, some fully correct, and a majority got the January and February trade payables right.
In 1(c) and 2(d), nearly all gave the advice, and most backed it with at least three valid points.
The profit or loss calculations in 2(b) and 2(c) were done to a high standard, and most split the overheads correctly.
In 2(a), a significant number defined a cost driver well and earned the mark.
mistakes: The March and April trade payables in 1(a) often had errors, and some left out the opening balance.
A few treated each month separately without carrying the balance forward.
The revised budget in 1(b) had considerably fewer fully correct answers, and relatively few got the trade payables right.
The scrap value in 2(b) and the revenue in 2(c) were the most common errors.
Some did not attempt 2(e), and overall it was answered less well than the rest of Question 2.
fix: Start each month with the closing balance from the month before.
Follow the supplier payment rule in the source exactly, carrying any unpaid amount to the next month.
Value returned units at scrap value, not at the selling price.
Recalculate revenue when the number of good units changes.
Attempt every part, even short comment questions.

questions.issue: Errors in March and April payables, missing opening balance, and a few months not linked.
questions.fix: Begin with the 3 000 bank balance and 27 100 payables, pay suppliers only as far as the 2 000 overdraft limit allows, and carry the rest forward.

questions.topic: Revised cash budget with half cash purchases
questions.issue: Many applied the discount and got the cash purchases right, but relatively few got the trade payables right.
questions.fix: Cash purchases are half of each month's purchases less 5%, so January is 28 600 x 0.5 x 0.95 = 13 585. Then pay suppliers for the credit half only as far as the overdraft limit allows.

questions.topic: Profit or loss per product under ABC
questions.issue: The most common error was the scrap figure.
questions.fix: Scrap is returned units x 8: 500 x 8 = 4 000 for product A and 600 x 8 = 4 800 for product B.

questions.issue: The most common error was revenue.
questions.fix: With no returns every unit sells at full price: 2 500 x 50 = 125 000 for A and 4 600 x 72 = 331 200 for B.

questions.topic: Suitability of the cost driver for the cameras
questions.issue: Some did not attempt it, and performance was below the rest of the question.
questions.fix: Scheme points: the driver does not change total profit, the camera cost is not linked to the number of inspections, and workers or labour hours might suit better.

quote.text: Accurate diagrams are a fundamental skill in economics

takeaways: Explain every point. On Paper 22 and Paper 42, answers that stated an effect without the reason behind it were held at low marks.
Evaluation means questioning the statement. On Paper 42 most who tried the collusion essay accepted the claim without testing it, and very few earned evaluation marks.
Draw the diagram the question needs and label it properly: real GDP and price level for AD/AS, a consumption externality for air travel, and the surplus on a minimum price.

On Paper 12 the macro questions were much harder than the micro ones, and on both multiple choice papers some of the weakest questions needed a calculation. Work through each figure on paper before you choose.
Revise the whole new syllabus. On Paper 22 the circular flow essay was among the weakest, and the report suggests this may be because the topic was new.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: Questions 10 and 13, both micro, each had a success rate above 80 per cent.
Just one micro question had a success rate below 40 per cent.
mistakes: Macro was much harder: seven of the fifteen macro questions had a success rate below 40 per cent.
Questions 16, 26, 27 and 29, all macro, had success rates under 30 per cent.
On Question 29, 56 per cent claimed the inflation rate could not be judged, although the table showed it was positive throughout.
fix: Give the macro topics as much practice time as the micro ones.
In national income questions, decide which items are flows of income and which are not, then add and subtract with care.
For a supply-side question, sketch an AS/AD diagram and shift AS to the right before you choose.

questions.topic: Net national income from national accounts
questions.issue: Only 21 per cent chose A, 19 billion. 43 per cent chose B, 25 billion, which leaves capital consumption in.
questions.fix: Start with GDP of 28, add net property income from abroad of minus 3, take off capital consumption of 6: 19. National debt is not income, so leave it out.

questions.issue: Only 18 per cent chose B, high unemployment with a rising price level. 53 per cent chose C, low unemployment with a stable price level.
questions.fix: Shifting AS to the right lowers unemployment and the price level, so it helps most when unemployment is high and prices are rising.

questions.topic: Why a government might prefer floating exchange rates
questions.issue: Only 28 per cent chose A, more independence in policy making.
questions.fix: Ask which option is really a benefit of floating rates. The others claim things floating rates do not deliver, such as more confidence in future prices.

questions.topic: Inflation and growth from GDP indices
questions.issue: Only 25 per cent chose C. 56 per cent chose A, which says the inflation rate cannot be told.
questions.fix: Money GDP rises faster than real GDP each year, so inflation is positive. Real GDP grows 5 per cent, then about 1 per cent, so growth is declining.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: Most candidates seemed to have enough time, and very few rubric errors were seen.
Question 1(a) was answered well overall, and most knew in 1(c) that higher interest rates reduce AD.
In 3(a), many gave at least two reasons for income inequality and explained them.
Question 4(b) on economic growth was far better answered than 4(a), and many reached at least level 2.
In 5(a), most knew that a floating rate is set by supply and demand, and in 5(b) supply-side policies were generally explained soundly.
mistakes: More answers scored under half marks, which the report thinks may come from the larger share of evaluation marks.
Points were stated, not explained, and evaluation was often a plain summary that earned nothing.
In 1(b) some copied the stimulus details without saying it was expansionary fiscal or AD policy, and many scored nothing.
In 2(a), most who tried it had a weak grasp of what price does in allocating resources, and many drifted into market against planned economies.
In 5(a), a surprising number did not say that appreciation means a rise in the currency's value, and very few explained why it might rise.
In 5(b), supply-side policies were seldom linked to the current account deficit, so most stopped around the middle of level 2.
fix: Match your time to the marks. Do not overspend on the short questions in Question 1.
Use the data in data response answers, and refer to it accurately.
Explain why each point matters for the question, for example why a price rise for exports is a problem for the current account.
For consider and assess questions, weigh at least two views and base the judgement on your own analysis.
Cover the whole syllabus, new topics such as the open economy circular flow included.

questions.topic: Comparing US inflation in two periods
questions.issue: Too much time went on describing every rise and fall, and occasionally the two periods were never actually compared.
questions.fix: Compare the trend: from 1.0 to 1.4 per cent and fairly stable in the first period, rising much faster from 1.4 to 5.4 per cent in the second.

questions.issue: The reason was often missing, so marks were often held at 2, and most gave no evaluation.
questions.fix: Say borrowing costs more and saving pays more, so consumption and investment fall, and AD falls. Evaluate with interest elasticity, confidence or cost-push inflation.

questions.topic: Whether the demand side or the supply side caused rising inflation, with an AD/AS diagram
questions.issue: The most frequent error was no diagram, or one with wrong axes or S and D instead of AS and AD. Most were capped at 5.
questions.fix: Label the axes real GDP and price level, draw AS and AD, link each shift to the data, and support your judgement.

questions.issue: Many listed effects without saying why each was good or bad, and many reached only 2 marks.
questions.fix: For each effect, say why it helps or harms the economy, cover positives too, and judge beyond a summary.

questions.topic: Functions of price in resource allocation
questions.issue: Not well answered. Answers were vague, and good ones were rare.
questions.fix: Explain rationing, signalling and incentives to producers, then say why they matter for a market economy.

questions.issue: Many left out the diagram. Some drew a maximum price, or did not mark the surplus.
questions.fix: Draw the minimum price above equilibrium, mark the surplus, and explain why the surplus is a problem.

questions.topic: Circular flow in a closed and an open economy
questions.issue: Least popular and among the least well done. Many thought a closed economy has no government, and hardly any gave the equilibrium condition.
questions.fix: Remember a closed economy still has government. Show that opening it adds imports as a leakage and exports as an injection.

questions.topic: Appreciation of a floating exchange rate
questions.issue: A surprising number gave no diagram, and points such as exports falling were asserted without the conditions that make them true.
questions.fix: Draw a labelled diagram showing the rise in value, say what causes it, and explain when each effect would happen.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Questions 1, 7, 8, 15, 18, 19 and 24 were answered correctly by at least 80 per cent of candidates.
Those high scoring questions came from across the syllabus and tested a range of skills.
mistakes: Fewer than half got Questions 2, 3, 6, 16 and 26 right.
In Question 16, the 35 per cent who chose A may have taken off sales tax as well as income tax and ignored the cash benefits.
In Question 26, the 26 per cent who chose D may not have noticed that the question asks what is added beyond measures of growth.
fix: Use marginal utility divided by price when choosing a utility maximising combination.
Measure the income effect between two parallel budget lines, not from the old point to the new one.
Keep sales tax out of disposable income, since it is paid when the income is spent.

questions.issue: Only 32 per cent chose B, 2 units of S and 1 of T. The rest split fairly evenly across A, C and D.
questions.fix: Divide marginal utility by price: the second unit of S gives 24 / 6 = 4 and the first unit of T gives 32 / 8 = 4. The ratios match at 2 of S and 1 of T.

questions.topic: Substitution and income effects on a diagram
questions.issue: 46 per cent chose B. 38 per cent chose A, which says the income effect is positive, and may have read it from E1 to E2.
questions.fix: The budget line pivots from FG to FH, so the price of X falls. Read the income effect from where the dotted line touches I1 to E2. Here it is negative.

questions.topic: Monopolistic competition in the long run
questions.issue: 37 per cent chose A, no allocative efficiency and no supernormal profit. 40 per cent chose C, which claims allocative efficiency.
questions.fix: There is no supernormal profit in the long run, but the profit-maximising point is not allocatively efficient.

questions.topic: Disposable income after tax and benefits
questions.issue: 40 per cent chose C, 60 per cent. 35 per cent chose A, 30 per cent.
questions.fix: 100 minus 45 per cent income tax leaves 55, plus 5 per cent cash benefits gives 60. Sales tax comes later, out of spending.

questions.issue: 37 per cent chose C. 29 per cent chose B, which counts only poverty as extra, and 26 per cent chose D, which also counts real income per capita as an extra component.
questions.fix: Real income per capita is already used to measure growth, so the extras are changes in the distribution of GDP and the level of poverty, both of them.

papers.title: A Level data response and essays
well: Question 1(b) on why governments borrow was generally answered well, and many gained at least 4 of the 5 marks.
Question 2 showed that many had studied negative externalities thoroughly, and their analysis had real depth.
About half chose Question 4, and a good share of them earned fairly high marks for knowledge, understanding and analysis.
Question 5 separated candidates well, and many recognised that not every part of globalisation raises living standards.
mistakes: Marks were consistently lower than in recent years, and few reached level 3 on the generic part.
Many diagrams were inaccurate, and analysis often stopped at a single simple chain, which kept answers at level 2.
A significant number did not use their analysis to reach a judgement, so evaluation often stayed at level 1.
In 1(d), many comments were not based on the article and earned nothing, and very few used the graph.
On Question 2, a significant number drew a production externality diagram for air travel, which is a consumption externality.
fix: Develop each argument through several linked steps, not one.
When a statement is followed by evaluate, test whether it is true, and say when it might not be.
In data response, use only the evidence in the article when the question says so.
Check whether an externality comes from production or consumption before you draw.
Build your conclusion from the arguments you have already made.

questions.issue: Many missed one of the three parts and listed things linked to recessions, such as high unemployment.
questions.fix: The scheme gives a mark each for linking it to GDP, a fall in GDP or output, and lasting two quarters.

questions.topic: Crowding out of the private sector
questions.issue: The report sets out what was needed rather than what went wrong: a clear meaning and the process behind it.
questions.fix: Show the steps the report lists: the government sells securities, interest rates rise, borrowing costs more, and private investment is crowded out.

questions.topic: Whether the article makes a conclusive case for high borrowing
questions.issue: Many comments came from outside the article. Very few used Fig. 1 to show the debt ratio was not stable.
questions.fix: Use the article: interest rates, the stability of the debt to GDP ratio, and different economies. Argue both sides, then conclude.

questions.topic: Government intervention to correct air travel externalities
questions.issue: A significant number treated it as a production externality, so the diagram and analysis went wrong.
questions.fix: Draw a negative consumption externality with overconsumption, then judge how far each intervention can correct it.

questions.topic: Collusion in oligopoly, prices and efficiency
questions.issue: The majority got no more than 8 of 14 for analysis, and most who tried it did not question the statement.
questions.fix: Explain how collusion makes the market behave like a monopoly, then question the claim using economies of scale, investment or regulation.

questions.topic: Expenditure-reducing policies, the balance of payments deficit and unemployment
questions.issue: Some did not question the statement, and many made no attempt at evaluation.
questions.fix: Analyse how lower AD cuts imports and raises cyclical unemployment, then ask how far, given the state of the economy and the type of unemployment.

questions.topic: Globalisation and living standards in low-income countries
questions.issue: Features of low-income countries were often mentioned but not built into the answer.
questions.fix: Show globalisation as trade plus capital, labour and technology, link it to features such as reliance on primary exports, and weigh benefits against harms.

quote.text: inappropriate abbreviations should be avoided

takeaways: Name the other account in every ledger entry. On Paper 22, details such as received cheque or bank transfers from customers cost marks where the account name, such as Bank, was needed.
Write names and labels in full. Shortened partner names and headings in an appropriation account lost marks on Paper 22.
For every advise question on Paper 22, give points on both sides and then a clear recommendation. A number of candidates wrote about one side only.
Show the working for every ratio, give the number of decimal places the question asks for, and add the % sign, times or :1 as needed.
On Paper 12, practise suspense account balances, the effect of inventory errors and club cost of sales. Some candidates seemed to find those items hard.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many candidates showed a good grasp of double entry and picked the key on many items.
Question 1, on the purpose of accounting, was found relatively straightforward, and many got it right.
The majority answered Question 4 on recording purchases returns correctly, and many knew the $180 credited to the supplier in Question 7.
Candidates generally did well on Questions 9 and 32, despite both looking demanding.
Most chose the right options on Questions 8, 21 and 25.
mistakes: Some seemed to find Question 11 hard and missed the suspense account balance before the corrections.
Some missed the effect of leaving goods out of closing inventory in Question 20.
Some chose a wrong cost of sales for the golf club refreshments in Question 27.
fix: Read each item slowly before choosing. The report stresses knowing exactly what is asked.
Work out how far each error has thrown the debit and credit totals out, then decide which side the suspense balance sits on.
Remember that lower closing inventory means higher cost of sales, so gross profit and equity both fall.
For club refreshments, find purchases from payments and the change in payables, then adjust for the change in inventory.

questions.issue: The majority answered correctly.
questions.fix: The key is C: the return goes on the debit side of Zuri's account and the credit side of purchases returns.

questions.topic: Trade and cash discount on a credit purchase
questions.issue: Many chose correctly.
questions.fix: The key is B, $180: take off the $20 trade discount, but not the cash discount, which is only given if payment is prompt.

questions.topic: Items on the wrong side of a trial balance
questions.issue: This was fairly demanding, yet candidates generally did well.
questions.fix: The key is A. Check each item: liabilities such as the bank loan, trade payables and overdraft belong on the credit side, and expenses and opening inventory on the debit side.

questions.issue: Some seemed to find it hard and did not choose the key.
questions.fix: A cheque received credited to bank leaves debits short by 2 x 280 = 560. The missing entry in Nunu's account leaves them short by 50. Total 610, so the key is D, $610 debit.

questions.topic: Goods left out of closing inventory
questions.issue: Some found it hard and did not choose the key.
questions.fix: Closing inventory too low makes cost of sales too high, so the key is D: gross profit and equity are both understated.

questions.topic: Club cost of sales of refreshments
questions.issue: Some chose the key, but others found it hard and chose a wrong option.
questions.fix: Purchases: 7 200 minus 250 owed at the start plus 400 owed at the end = 7 350. Inventory fell by 100, so add it: 7 450, option D.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Most candidates appeared to know the topics and attempted every question, and many scripts were neat.
Most showed a good understanding of the three-column cash book and earned good marks.
Many earned high marks on the correcting journal entries in 2(a).
The majority knew control accounts well, and many earned both marks for two advantages in 3(c).
The partnership appropriation account in 5(a) was popular, and many earned full marks.
mistakes: Some ledger and book entries used descriptions instead of account names, and short forms such as S for Samir or Int appeared in some appropriation accounts.
Ratio workings were sometimes missing or impossible to trace in 4(a).
In the three advise questions, a number of candidates wrote about one side only.
Few got the corrected profit in 2(c) fully right. Common errors were leaving out the draft profit or including error 5.
In 4(b), a significant number thought the given ratios were for this year, not the year before.
Many did not link the going concern principle to why external users want to see the accounts.
fix: Write the date, the account name and the amount for every entry.
Plan each advise answer as a short list: points for, points against, then a recommendation.
Say whether a ratio has improved or worsened, not just whether it went up or down.
Read every line of data carefully, including which year each figure belongs to.
Leave out items that do not belong in an account, such as cash sales in a sales ledger control account.

questions.issue: Errors included wrong discount amounts, transaction descriptions as details, treating the contra as drawings, balancing the discount columns, and a credit balance on the cash column.
questions.fix: Use account names as details, total the discount columns without balancing them, and remember cash in hand cannot be a credit balance.

questions.topic: Why external users care that the business continues (going concern)
questions.issue: Many missed the link to going concern, and answers on government often turned to the economy or subsidies.
questions.fix: The scheme links each user to paying: the bank manager to repaying a loan or overdraft, the government to paying tax, and trade payables to paying for goods.

questions.issue: On error 2 some did not double the amount, on error 3 some used the suspense account, and on error 4 some wrongly doubled it.
questions.fix: Error 2 debits purchases and credits Stella with 2 x 247 = 494. Error 3 debits sales and credits rent with no suspense entry. Error 4 needs only 75.

questions.issue: Few were wholly correct. Some left out the draft profit or included error 5, which has no effect on profit.
questions.fix: Start from the draft profit of 9 800, take off 200 and 494, add back 75: 9 181.

questions.topic: Selling equipment to pay a supplier
questions.issue: A number gave one side only. A number also wrongly mentioned a loss on sale or an effect on production.
questions.fix: The equipment is fully depreciated, so selling it for 2 500 gives a profit, not a loss. Weigh paying most of the debt against replacing the equipment later.

questions.topic: Gross margin, profit margin, inventory turnover and liquid ratio
questions.issue: Errors included wrong opening inventory, leaving out other income, including inventory in the liquid ratio, and missing units.
questions.fix: Opening inventory is half of 7 500, so 3 750. Cost of sales 3 750 + 62 305 minus 7 500 = 58 555, and turnover 58 555 / 5 625 = 10.41 times. Liquid ratio 9 240 : 10 500 = 0.88:1.

questions.topic: Time gap before financial statements are ready
questions.issue: Many did not see how the gap could limit a pricing decision.
questions.fix: The trader needs the profit made since the year end and the inventory held now before deciding.

questions.topic: Partner paying private car expenses from the business
questions.issue: Many got the drawings and interest on drawings right, but the effect on profit gave more trouble.
questions.fix: Private expenses paid by the business are drawings, so profit for the year is not affected, while drawings and interest on drawings rise.

quote.text: Careful reading of the stem might have prevented this

takeaways: Read who the question is about. On Paper 22, a small proportion wrote about an MNC's home country instead of its host, and some explained why farmers earn little instead of why low incomes mean low living standards.
When Section A gives you a table, use its figures. On Paper 22 Question 1(f), some wrote in general terms about spending and unemployment and never analysed the table.
For the 8 mark discuss questions, Level 3 needs both sides explained in depth. On 4(d), some only stated points, such as population growth causing unemployment, without saying why.
If the task is only to draw, the diagram is the whole answer. On Paper 22 Question 1(e), a relatively high number also wrote an explanation and could have saved that time.

On Paper 12, check formulas and definitions before choosing. Common wrong answers seem to have come from an inverted elasticity formula, one negative quarter taken as a recession, and an inflation rate read as a price level.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: A large majority answered Questions 1, 2, 3, 10, 17, 20, 22, 26 and 28 correctly.
They were spread across the syllabus and tested a range of skills.
mistakes: Questions 8, 9, 12, 16, 19, 24 and 27 had the fewest correct answers, again spread across the syllabus.
On Question 24, half chose the option about the price level being highest in year 1, which the report calls a popular misconception about inflation rates.
On Question 27, a quarter chose quarter 3, which suggests they took a single quarter of falling output as a recession.
fix: Write the elasticity formula down before putting numbers in.
A fall in the inflation rate still means prices are rising, as long as the rate stays above zero.
A recession needs two quarters in a row of negative growth.
Check whether a table column shows a total or an average before working anything out.

questions.topic: Price rise needed with a PED of 0.5
questions.issue: 64 per cent chose D, 20 per cent. 23 per cent chose A, 5 per cent, which appears to come from turning the formula upside down.
questions.fix: PED is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price. So 0.5 = 10 / price change, and the price must rise by 20 per cent.

questions.topic: Immediate effect of a maximum price on bread
questions.issue: 61 per cent chose C, a shortage. 20 per cent chose A, a shift of the demand curve to the right.
questions.fix: A maximum price below equilibrium does not move either curve. Demand is greater than supply at that price, so there is a shortage.

questions.issue: 64 per cent chose A, average fixed cost falls. 31 per cent chose D, average variable cost rises, which seems to come from reading the total variable cost column as an average.
questions.fix: Divide fixed cost of 1 000 by output and it falls. Dividing total variable cost by output shows average variable cost falling too, from 10 to 6.25.

questions.issue: 62 per cent chose B, firms expand to meet higher demand. 26 per cent chose A, which says consumers borrow less.
questions.fix: More money, lower interest rates or a weaker currency would not reduce borrowing. They raise spending, so firms expand.

questions.issue: Only 31 per cent chose D, which says money lost real value in three of the years. 50 per cent chose C.
questions.fix: Inflation was positive in three years and negative in one, so money lost value in three years. The line shows the rate of change, not the price level.

questions.issue: 55 per cent chose D, quarter 4. 25 per cent chose C, quarter 3.
questions.fix: Real GDP was 100, 101, 99 and 98, so output fell in quarters 3 and 4. Only after quarter 4 are there two falls in a row.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Question 1 stayed strong, and most made good use of the data. There were some excellent scripts.
Most used their time sensibly, and the vast majority answered every required question.
In 1(b) the majority found both causes and kept the answer brief, and 1(e) had many clear, well labelled diagrams.
Good answers to 1(h) were common, and many used the source to show who gains from growth and who may lose.
Question 4 was relatively well answered, and in 5(c) candidates picked up on the word not and gave a range of reasons.
mistakes: In 1(g), some were confused about the central bank, and a number had it using fiscal policy.
In 2(c), some wrote mainly about discouraging demerit goods instead of encouraging merit goods.
In 3(a), a number confused a minimum price with a maximum price, or called it the lowest price that still makes a profit.
In 4(a), some confused productivity with production.
In 4(c), some mixed up the current account with the government's budget balance.
In 5(a), some explained what price elasticity of demand means instead of naming two determinants, and a few gave supply determinants.
fix: Finish one question before starting the next. Jumping between parts of different questions tends to lose the focus.
Identify questions such as 1(b) can be answered briefly.
Use the data in Section A, especially for the relationship question.
Stay on the exact point of the question in the (d) parts, and explain both sides in depth for Level 3.
Link every effect back to what the question asks about, such as the current account or macroeconomic aims.

questions.topic: Value of US imports from China in 2020
questions.issue: A number wrote 560 dollars without the billion.
questions.fix: Give the unit: $560 billion. Check the size of every figure you copy from a table.

questions.topic: Diagram for a rise in the price of a complement to ice cream
questions.issue: Some confused the demand and supply curves, and some shifted demand to the right.
questions.fix: Label price and quantity, show the original curves, shift demand to the left, and mark both equilibria.

questions.topic: Relationship between government spending and unemployment
questions.issue: Some wrote in general terms and did not analyse the table.
questions.fix: Name the main inverse relationship, give figures from the table, point out the exception year and explain why.

questions.topic: Whether a central bank should aim for low inflation
questions.issue: Candidates found it quite challenging, and some had the central bank using fiscal policy.
questions.fix: Weigh the benefits of low inflation against the costs of the contractionary monetary policy needed to reach it, such as higher interest rates.

questions.topic: Whether growth benefits everyone in the US
questions.issue: Some discussed growth in general, for example the current account, without asking whether everyone gains.
questions.fix: Show which groups gain, through higher incomes and jobs, and which may not, for example because income is unevenly shared.

questions.topic: Benefits an MNC brings to its host country
questions.issue: Not all explained the benefits, and a small proportion wrote about the home country.
questions.fix: Underline host country. For each benefit, name it and then explain its effect: the scheme gives one mark for each.

questions.topic: Why low income farmers have low living standards
questions.issue: Some answered a different question, explaining why farmers earn little.
questions.fix: Start from the low income and follow its effects, for example being unable to afford good healthcare or housing, and so poorer health.

questions.issue: Some stopped at lower costs and prices without reaching the current account.
questions.fix: Continue the chain: lower prices and better quality make exports more competitive, so exports rise and imports fall.

quote.text: No candidate provided an effective evaluation for this question.

takeaways: On Papers 11, 12 and 14, part (e) has no application marks. It gives 2 for knowledge, 2 for analysis and 2 for evaluation, so a justified decision matters.
Read the whole question. On Paper 11, 3(d) asked for the effect on CPK, and naming the change was not enough.
Learn precise definitions, and revise every topic. Papers 11, 12 and 14 each had terms or topics that caught candidates out.
On the case study papers, copying figures or facts from an appendix earns nothing until you explain what they mean for the business.
Use a different case detail for each point, and in a (b) recommendation say why the other options lose.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: The definition and knowledge parts, (a) and (b), went better on the whole this session.
Opportunity cost in 2(a) was well answered by many.
Many gave clear definitions of non-current assets in 3(a), and many gained both marks in 3(b).
Many understood methods of internal communication well in 2(e).
mistakes: Some definitions were not precise enough, most of all recession in 4(a).
Weak knowledge of business terms led to low marks on 1(d), 3(e) and 4(e).
There was some evidence that candidates did not read the entire question, as in 3(d).
In 2(e) a mark of 2 was common, because many named methods without developing them.
In 3(c), effects such as wage rises or redundancy were not direct results of a tax rise, so they earned nothing.
fix: Use the stem for application in the part (c) and (d) questions that name the business. 1(c) needed none.
Part (e) carries no application marks, so spend the effort developing two points and a decision that follows from them.
Do not repeat earlier points as your evaluation. Add a reason the decision is right.
Underline the command and the focus, such as effect on the business, before you write.

questions.issue: Some described training for new workers, which is induction, and earned nothing.
questions.fix: Say it is training done at work, learning the job alongside an experienced employee.

questions.issue: Many were unclear on the method and often divided output by the variable cost per unit.
questions.fix: Multiply $80 by the output of 12 000 to get $960 000, and show the working.

questions.topic: Advantage and disadvantage of quality control
questions.issue: Not well understood by many. Many said it would stop all errors, not seeing that only some products are checked. Two applications were hard to find.
questions.fix: An advantage is catching faults before phones reach customers. A disadvantage is that it does not show where the fault began.

questions.topic: New features as an extension strategy
questions.issue: Many wrote about a completely new product. Only the strongest saw a problem, such as customers disliking the changes.
questions.fix: Weigh more appeal and sales against the risk to loyal customers, and compare with another strategy such as new markets.

questions.topic: Limitations of number of employees as a measure of size
questions.issue: Many struggled, often listing other measures of size, such as profit or output, instead of limitations.
questions.fix: Give limitations such as having many part-time staff, or capital intensive production that needs few workers.

questions.issue: One of the hardest questions. A common error was saying shareholders pay no debts, missing that their invested money can be lost.
questions.fix: Say shareholders can lose only what they invested, so their personal assets are safe if the electricity business fails.

questions.topic: Effects on CPK of a fall in two ratios
questions.issue: Many only said both ratios fell, with figures. Very few explained what the falls would mean for CPK.
questions.fix: Go on to the effect, such as trouble paying short-term liabilities, or a need to raise prices at the 5 clubs.

questions.issue: Many knew the terms in general but not how they motivate. Some confused job enrichment with job rotation.
questions.fix: Explain how each motivates, such as feeling valued or money as a reward, then justify which suits a business better.

questions.issue: Many gave two examples of expenses, which is one reason, so 2 marks was the most. Some said it would buy the franchise.
questions.fix: Give two different reasons, such as paying day to day expenses and coping with emergencies, each linked to the salon.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Many showed good knowledge of concepts, and parts (a) and (b) were generally well attempted.
Most knew ways to increase added value in 1(c), and 2(c) on why cash matters was well answered by most.
There were some excellent answers to 2(e) on advertising in specialist magazines.
Most knew democratic leadership well in 3(d), and many showed good knowledge and application in 4(d).
mistakes: Many lacked precision in definitions, and many simply reordered the words of market share.
Many missed application marks, and many still put analysis in part (c) and application in part (e).
Where evaluation was attempted, most decisions lacked a supporting reason.
Repeating one point in other words, or reusing the same application, only counted once.
3(e) on government spending was poorly answered by many, and effective evaluation was rare.
fix: Match your answer to the skills on offer: part (c) never rewards analysis, and part (e) never rewards application.
Any part of the syllabus can appear, so leave no topic out of revision.
Pick one option, back it with a reason, and show where the alternative falls down.
Develop a point by saying what follows from it. More customers and more sales are the same point.

questions.topic: Definition of statement of financial position
questions.issue: Most left out that it shows a point in time. Some confused it with an income statement or a cash flow forecast.
questions.fix: Say it records what the business owns and owes, valued on one particular date.

questions.topic: Advantages to EQR of selling franchises
questions.issue: A common mistake was writing about what franchisees gain instead of EQR as franchisor, and others made vague claims about growth or profit.
questions.fix: Use points such as the $85 000 fee for each franchise, a share of franchisee profit, or faster growth to lift the 6 per cent market share.

questions.issue: Working out the gross profit margin in place of the profit margin was a common mistake.
questions.fix: Divide profit for the year by revenue and multiply by 100: 72 divided by 480 gives 15%. This scheme needed the % sign for both marks.

questions.issue: Challenging. Only the strongest explained the smaller percentage change in demand, and a common mistake was giving reasons for high prices.
questions.fix: Give reasons such as no close substitutes or the product being a necessity, then explain the effect of a price change.

questions.issue: Poorly answered by many. A common mistake was giving features of good communication instead of its benefits.
questions.fix: Give benefits such as fewer mistakes or better coordination between departments.

questions.topic: Factors in choosing who to make redundant
questions.issue: Many repeated points in new words, some were vague, and some gave reasons for redundancy instead.
