questions.fix: Give four separate factors, such as whether the role is still needed, attendance record, length of service and pay.

questions.topic: Whether all businesses gain from more government spending
questions.issue: Many gave no benefit or drawback to a business, writing about consumers or the economy instead.
questions.fix: Weigh gains such as more sales or grants against higher taxes raising costs, then decide.

questions.issue: Most found this hard. Answers tended to list extra features instead of the difference, and most did not link it to TYA.
questions.fix: Set one feature against its opposite, such as limited against unlimited liability, and tie it to the car maker.

questions.topic: Legal controls as a location factor
questions.issue: Poorly answered. Many could not give effects of legal controls, and a common mistake was choosing demand or competition as factors.
questions.fix: Weigh legal controls against factors such as labour or raw materials. This general question needs no application.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Many knew the concepts well, and the opening (a) and (b) parts generally went well.
Most correctly classified raw materials and insurance in 1(b), and 1(c) on a motivated workforce went well overall.
Most worked out the cash flow values in 2(b).
Reasons for expansion in 3(b) and the stages of the product life cycle in 4(b) were answered well by most.
mistakes: Many clearly did not understand legal controls over marketing, Kaizen or ethical issues well.
A significant number left 1(e) and 4(c) unanswered.
Many still wrote analysis where part (c) gives none, and application where part (e) gives none.
Of those who evaluated, most could not support their decision with reasons.
Repetition, such as two examples of the same cost, was a common mistake in 1(c), 2(a) and 3(c).
fix: Link (c) and (d) answers to the stem, using a different example for each point.
Do not define the term in part (e). Answer the judgement the question asks for.
Revise the whole syllabus, including topics that come up less often.
End part (e) by choosing, justifying the choice, and saying what makes the rejected option weaker.

questions.topic: Advantage and disadvantage of democratic leadership
questions.issue: A common mistake was confusing it with delegation, and some repeated the knowledge instead of developing it.
questions.fix: Use case details, for example asking 400 employees takes time, which can slow decisions.

questions.topic: Kaizen as the way to achieve lean production
questions.issue: Many were unfamiliar with Kaizen. Some wrote about flow or batch production, and a significant number did not attempt it.
questions.fix: Weigh Kaizen against another lean method, such as just-in-time, then judge which suits a manufacturer best.

questions.topic: Calculating figures in a cash flow forecast
questions.issue: Some found X harder, possibly because June's net cash flow was negative and needed working backwards.
questions.fix: X is the outflow that leaves a net cash flow of minus 2000 from an inflow of 1000, so X is 3000. Y is 500.

questions.issue: Challenging for most. Some confused it with other sources, gave mirror points, or assumed it raises large sums.
questions.fix: Use points such as testing public reaction or no guarantee of raising the full amount, linked to the new jewellery shop.

questions.issue: A common mistake was explaining primary methods. Some wrote about promotion instead.
questions.fix: Use methods such as government statistics or trade journals, and say what each tells Ayesha.

questions.issue: Challenging for most. Some confused it with revenue, and some deducted only expenses or only cost of sales.
questions.fix: Define it as total revenue minus total costs.

questions.topic: Changing suppliers as a response to child labour
questions.issue: A common mistake was assuming BHA used child labour itself, when it was a supplier. Some mixed up ethics and law.
questions.fix: Weigh protecting the brand image against the time and higher cost of finding new suppliers.

questions.topic: Advantage and disadvantage of quality control
questions.issue: A significant number wrote about the importance of quality rather than the merits of quality control, and many mixed it up with quality assurance.
questions.fix: Use points such as catching faults before customers buy, and the cost of employing inspectors.

papers.title: Case study
well: Preparation was generally sound, the overall standard good, and weak scripts very few.
The majority named and explained four objectives for SA in 1(a), linked to the case.
Knowledge of why quality matters in 2(a) was generally strong.
3(a) on being a sole trader was well answered, and 3(b) showed strong numeracy.
mistakes: The weakest topics were ecommerce and the effect of a rise in inflation.
Answers short of analysis and evaluation stayed in the lower level band.
Only a few gave a meaningful judgement on whether the opportunities of ecommerce outweighed the threats.
There was less confidence about leasing than about bank loans and retained profit.
Weaker answers to 3(b) copied the forecast data without using it.
fix: Let the marks on each question set how far you develop your answer.
Write as Tokumbo would think about SA, not as one of his staff would.
Before writing, picture the business: a small, young safari tour firm run by a sole trader.
In a recommendation, weigh short-term against long-term effects to lift it to Level 2 or Level 3.

questions.issue: Weaker answers gave strategies rather than objectives, sometimes copying from the case.
questions.fix: Pick objectives such as survival for a business only two years old, and explain why each suits SA.

questions.issue: Many saw direct booking without holiday companies, but only a few judged which effect would be greatest.
questions.fix: Weigh the saving on fees against the cost of a website good enough to beat many rivals, then decide.

questions.topic: Why quality matters to a business
questions.issue: Some weaker answers repeated points or wrote about why quality matters to customers instead of to the business.
questions.fix: Make four separate points with reasoning. This question had no application marks.

questions.topic: Leasing, bank loan or retained profit for new vehicles
questions.issue: Leasing was less well understood than the other two sources.
questions.fix: Note that leased vehicles are never SA's to sell, and that a young business may struggle to borrow enough at 2 per cent.

questions.topic: Advantage and disadvantage of being a sole trader
questions.issue: Some gave two advantages or two disadvantages, which limited the marks.
questions.fix: Give exactly one of each, explained and linked to Tokumbo's business.

questions.topic: Three options for growth, with calculations
questions.issue: Weaker answers copied the forecast tourist numbers and total costs, which earned nothing.
questions.fix: Calculate profit and average cost for each option, then use the results to choose and reject.

questions.topic: Effects of a rise in inflation
questions.issue: Some gave brief outcomes without the chain of reasoning, and without linking them to SA.
questions.fix: Trace the chain: dearer fuel and hotels, higher tour prices, then fewer bookings as tourists spend on basic needs.

questions.topic: Two methods of training for existing employees
questions.issue: The topic was widely known. The report reminds candidates that brief definitions and mirror statements earn nothing where developed points are needed.
questions.fix: Develop each method's effect on cost and reputation, then justify the choice for a small business.

papers.title: Case study
well: Candidates had generally been well prepared, and the majority seemed to have time to attempt every question.
Economies of scale and reduced competition were generally well explained in 1(a).
2(a) was answered well, and candidates knew the roles of packaging.
Overall, answers to 3(b) used the Appendix 2 data well.
mistakes: The least understood topics were globalisation, diseconomies of scale and how users of accounts use financial information.
Many (b) answers lacked analysis and evaluation, which kept them in the lower level.
In 1(b) many found it hard to develop points, and very few saw the threat of foreign rivals in the home market.
Diseconomies of scale in 3(a) were not widely known, and a number of candidates gave no response.
Most answers to 4(b) left the Appendix 3 figures unused, so few reached Level 3.
fix: Vary your case details across the sections of an (a) question, not chocolates every time.
Say why a point is an opportunity, threat, advantage or disadvantage for CC, not just what it is.
Make claims only where the insert gives evidence.
Consider consequences now and later in each recommendation, as the higher levels require.

questions.topic: Why the owners might want to expand
questions.issue: Some gave bare statements such as more profit, and weaker answers explained how to expand, not why.
questions.fix: Develop the chain, for example higher output of chocolate bars raising sales and so profit.

questions.issue: Many just listed points, and some weaker answers confused globalisation with selling abroad.
questions.fix: Explain each point, such as low wage production cutting unit costs, and include competition from abroad at home.

questions.issue: The application mark was not always gained, because every role used only chocolates as the example.
questions.fix: Use a different case detail for each of the four roles.

questions.issue: Some named the life cycle stages, then repeated the appendix. Weaker answers made claims about children and adults with no evidence.
questions.fix: Explain what each stage means for future sales of Tiabar and Choco, then justify which to drop.

questions.issue: Not widely known, with a number of no responses.
questions.fix: Give diseconomies such as poor communication, and explain why each pushes up unit costs.

questions.topic: Choosing the Operations Manager for NM
questions.issue: Weaker answers gave a plus and a minus for each manager without saying why it mattered to CC.
questions.fix: Use Appendix 2, such as Samuel's 10 years against Ritesh's 2, and say how each would affect the takeover.

questions.issue: Weaker answers stayed at one mark for each benefit, and some applied this generic question to the case.
questions.fix: Explain how each benefit helps the employee, such as support if unfairly dismissed.

questions.topic: Usefulness of financial statements to three stakeholders
questions.issue: The most challenging question. Most answers were general, and a few took the bank manager to be a CC employee.
questions.fix: Pick a figure from Appendix 3 for each group and say what decision it helps, such as whether to lend.

papers.title: Case study
well: Preparation was generally good, the overall standard was good, and few scripts were weak.
Many made a good start on 1(a), with reasons such as fewer tourists or a lack of experience.
3(a) on stakeholder objectives was generally well answered.
4(a) on working capital was generally well answered, with most saying it pays day to day expenses.
mistakes: The weakest topics were stages of the business cycle, methods of market research and why working capital matters.
Weaker answers copied appendix details without comment and earned nothing.
Answers missing analysis and evaluation were held in the lower level band.
In 2(b) the majority gained no application, and taxi could not count because it was in the question.
Some recommendations answered the wrong way round, such as which driver to keep.
fix: Read the question closely. A redundancy question asks who should go, not who should stay.
In 2(b), use details other than the word taxi, such as the drivers, to earn application.
Bring a fresh case reference into every section of an (a) answer.
Before you recommend, think about short-term and long-term effects on KAT.

questions.topic: Why KAT is at risk of failing
questions.issue: Answers were often applied, but full credit needed a full explanation of how each factor could cause failure.
questions.fix: Take each reason through to failure, for example falling demand leaving too little to pay fixed costs.

questions.issue: Several believed Samuel had the fewest hours, when he was available for the most, at 48.
questions.fix: Read the appendix closely and explain why each strength helps KAT, such as repeat customers.

questions.topic: Effects of the stages of the business cycle
questions.issue: A common error was writing about the product life cycle. No application was needed.
questions.fix: Explain what happens to demand and sales in growth, boom, recession and slump.

questions.topic: Mobile phone, email or meeting for urgent bookings
questions.issue: Only better answers went beyond simple points, and the majority gained no application.
questions.fix: Use details such as the drivers, and explain limits like email needing a connection and giving no sign it was read.

questions.issue: The local community was least well answered, and weaker answers described the group instead of its objective.
questions.fix: Give one objective per group, with a different case detail each time, not taxi services four times.

questions.topic: Most useful method of market research
questions.issue: Weaker answers gave only simple points, and some were too vague to show which method they meant.
questions.fix: Weigh each method for the new services, then say why the other two are less useful.

questions.issue: Weaker answers said working capital is for investment, and some did not say why each reason mattered.
questions.fix: Use reasons such as fuel and wages or a taxi repair, and explain the effect on KAT.

questions.issue: Weaker answers copied Appendix 3, and recommendations often listed points without allowing for the loan still to repay.
questions.fix: Take the loan left from the sale value, for example $10 000 less $7200 leaves $2800 for Vehicle A.

quote.text: This type of question often causes confusion

takeaways: A budget deficit is about government revenue and spending; a current account deficit is about trade. On Paper 22 some confused the two in Questions 1(e), 1(g) and 5(b).
Answer only the three optional questions you need on Paper 2. The Paper 22 report says doing all four leaves less time to write each answer well.
Say who gains. On Paper 23 many wrote host country benefits when asked about an MNC's home country, and some wrote about the countries workers move to instead of Ecuador.
In discuss questions, explain both sides with economic reasoning. Paper 22 says Level 3 needs depth, yet a number only stated points, and on Paper 23 the case for the other side was often thin.
On multiple choice, read the stem twice. On Paper 12 the not in Question 18 may have been missed, and on Paper 13 half or more chose the same wrong option in Questions 8, 13 and 23.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 7, 10, 16, 17 and 29 were answered correctly by at least 70 per cent of candidates.
They were spread over the syllabus and tested a mix of skills.
mistakes: Questions 6, 8, 18, 19, 22, 23 and 26 were answered correctly by under 40 per cent.
On Question 19, only 9 per cent saw that output was highest in the last year.
On Question 23, 64 per cent linked rising unemployment with rising inflation.
fix: A positive growth rate means output is still rising, even when the rate is lower than before.
Higher unemployment means weaker demand, so growth and inflation both tend to fall.
Separate absolute poverty, lacking the basics to live, from relative poverty, being poor compared with others nearby.

questions.topic: Diagram showing a shortage at price P
questions.issue: 39 per cent chose the key, A, so 61 per cent picked one of the other three diagrams. C was the most popular of those, at 26 per cent.
questions.fix: A shortage needs quantity demanded above quantity supplied at P. In diagram A, buyers want Q2 at P, but sellers supply only Q1.

questions.topic: Main purpose of a new toll road
questions.issue: Only 23 per cent chose A, tackling market failure. 52 per cent chose D, raising toll revenue.
questions.fix: The road was built to cut congestion. Congestion is an external cost, so the aim is to correct market failure, even though the toll also raises money.

questions.topic: What would not follow from lower interest rates
questions.issue: Only 28 per cent chose C, a fall in inflation. 34 per cent chose B, a fall in the currency's international value, and the report suggests some may not have noticed the word not.
questions.fix: Lower rates encourage borrowing and spending, which can push prices up. So a fall in inflation is the result that would not be expected.

questions.topic: Output from an economic growth rate chart
questions.issue: Only 9 per cent chose C, output highest in year 5. The other three options each drew around 30 per cent.
questions.fix: Read the chart as a rate of change, not a level. A positive rate, even a falling one, still adds to output, and the report says the gains in the other years more than make up for year 4, so output is highest in year 5.

questions.issue: Only 23 per cent chose D, more trade union power. 36 per cent chose C, a higher interest rate.
questions.fix: Stronger unions push for pay rises, extra pay raises spending, and higher demand pulls prices up.

questions.topic: Effects of rising unemployment on growth and inflation
questions.issue: Only 21 per cent chose A, both falling. 64 per cent chose B, growth falling with inflation rising.
questions.fix: Rising unemployment goes with falling growth, and weaker demand means prices tend to fall too.

questions.issue: 38 per cent chose C, fewer homeless people. 27 per cent chose D, a lower rate of inflation, and 24 per cent chose B, lower income tax.
questions.fix: Lower inflation or income tax may affect relative poverty. Housing the homeless meets a basic need, so it cuts absolute poverty.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 2, 14, 19 and 26 were answered correctly by at least 75 per cent of candidates.
Apart from four questions, results were well within the expected range.
mistakes: Questions 7, 8, 13 and 23 were answered correctly by under 35 per cent.
On Question 13, 56 per cent chose higher income tax rates as the cause of lower real income.
On Question 23, 57 per cent chose the claim that everyone always uses public goods.
fix: Sort factors into those that affect elasticity of supply and those that affect elasticity of demand.
Market failure still has an equilibrium. It is just not the best one for society.
Real income means income adjusted for prices, so look for the option that must cut it.
Watch for absolute words such as always, which often make an option wrong.

questions.topic: Factor influencing price elasticity of supply
questions.issue: 34 per cent chose B, spare capacity. 31 per cent chose C, the price of substitutes, which affects demand.
questions.fix: Spare capacity lets firms raise output quickly. Necessity, substitutes and share of income are demand factors.

questions.issue: 33 per cent chose C, too few merit goods supplied. 50 per cent chose B, continuing disequilibrium.
questions.fix: A failing market still settles at an equilibrium, just not the social optimum. Too few merit goods is the consequence.

questions.topic: Loss of real income for union members
questions.issue: 32 per cent chose D. 56 per cent chose A, higher income tax rates.
questions.fix: Higher tax cuts disposable income, but wages may have risen or prices fallen. Only wages adjusted for inflation falling makes the loss certain, so D.

questions.topic: Why a government provides public goods
questions.issue: 28 per cent chose B, not profitable for private firms. 57 per cent chose A, which may come from mixing up can be used by everyone with always used by everyone.
questions.fix: Private firms cannot charge users, so they will not supply public goods for profit. That is why the government steps in.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: A relatively high number did well on the compulsory Question 1, and most found the naira figure correctly in 1(a).
Answers to 1(f) keep improving. A relatively high proportion named the inverse relationship, gave evidence and spotted the exception.
Question 2 was the most popular, and most gave a precise definition of opportunity cost in 2(a).
Question 3(c) on spending cuts and poverty was well answered, with good links to welfare payments and subsidies.
General performance on 4(d) was good, and some answers to 5(c) were excellent.
mistakes: There appeared to be a rise in the share answering all four optional questions, which leaves less time for each one.
Some (d) answers were very brief, or stated points and unlikely outcomes without saying why.
Some confused productivity with production, and a number mixed up minimum and maximum prices in 1(h).
In 1(b), not all used the source, and in 1(d) a small proportion just repeated the question's words.
In 4(b), a number confused public goods with merit goods, free goods or basic necessities.
In 5(d), a small proportion wrote about a rise in interest rates instead of a fall, and some confused saving with investment.
fix: Choose three optional questions and spend the saved time developing each answer.
Build chains of links in the (c) and (d) parts, for example from education cuts to lower skills to lower future earnings.
Use the source whenever Question 1 tells you to.
Read the exact wording before defining. Question 4(a) asked about supply, not demand.
For the data question, give the relationship, evidence, the exception and a reason.

questions.issue: A small proportion skipped it, and some multiplied 6 400 by 400.
questions.fix: At 400 naira to the dollar, divide: 6 400 / 400 = $16.

questions.topic: Effect of higher unemployment on the government's budget
questions.issue: A small proportion wrote about exports and imports, confusing the budget with the current account.
questions.fix: Tax revenue falls as incomes, profits and spending fall, and spending on benefits may rise, so a deficit is likely to grow.

questions.topic: Whether a farm subsidy would cut the current account deficit
questions.issue: Some wrote about government spending and tax, and a small number confused it with a bank current account.
questions.fix: Link the subsidy to lower costs and prices, more competitive exports, and net exports. Then ask whether demand abroad would really rise.

questions.issue: A small number confused progressive with regressive tax, and some wrote about regressive indirect taxes.
questions.fix: Both can take more money from the rich. The difference is the rate: it rises with income under a progressive system and stays the same under a proportional one.

questions.topic: Whether a fall in unemployment always helps workers
questions.issue: Some seemed to think lower unemployment would cut wages, or that more people in work must mean fewer hours each or others losing jobs.
questions.fix: Lower unemployment can mean firms compete for scarce workers and unions grow stronger. Weigh that against inflation eating into pay.

questions.issue: A number lacked precision, and a small number defined inelastic demand.
questions.fix: Quantity supplied changes by a smaller percentage than price.

questions.topic: Furniture market when the price of wood rises
questions.issue: Some stayed on the market for wood, and a small proportion confused the demand and supply curves.
questions.fix: Wood is a cost of furniture, so shift the furniture supply curve left. Show price rising and quantity falling, with labelled axes and both equilibria.

questions.issue: Some just said imported inflation without analysis, and some confused the effects on export and import prices.
questions.fix: Import prices rise, which raises costs and prices. Cheaper exports raise demand, which can pull prices up too.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: The majority wrote neatly and spaced their answers well.
The majority calculated 1(a) correctly, and 1(d) on the recession was generally well done.
Most found the positive relationship and the exception in 1(f), with far fewer purely descriptive comments than in past years.
A very high number gave a complete, accurate answer on the toothpaste market in 4(c).
Nearly all knew in 3(d) that lower unemployment means more people in work, and most understood productivity in 3(c).
mistakes: In 1(g), many said profits rose but mentioned only revenue, with no reference to costs, and few explained the wage, union and emigration points.
In 1(h), a few took emigration to mean workers entering the country, and others wrote about the countries receiving the workers.
In 2(d), why consumers might not benefit was weaker, and quite a few treated a competitive market as if it meant a market economy, writing about missing public and merit goods.
In 3(a), quite a few said an indirect tax is passed to a third party without saying how.
Many Question 5 candidates left 5(a) blank, which the report reads as a gap in knowledge of international trade.
A few limited 5(b) to why Palau itself is poorer than the US.
fix: Match the length of the answer to the command word: identify needs a few words, discuss needs both sides.
Stick to the number of points the question asks for, and explain each one well.
Use the Section B stimulus as a guide, but bring in other examples too.
For profits, discuss both revenue and costs.
Keep a clear gap between answers so the examiner can see where each new question starts.

questions.topic: Price elasticity of supply of oil
questions.issue: Quite a few wrote 16 per cent, and another common error was inverting the formula.
questions.fix: Percentage change in quantity supplied over percentage change in price: minus 8 / minus 50 = 0.16. The scheme does not accept 16 per cent.

questions.issue: Some gave for whom to produce, which had no example in the source, and some gave how much to produce.
questions.fix: Use what to produce and how to produce, which the source illustrates with less oil and more textiles, and fewer capital goods.

questions.issue: Some used material about the wider economy, and some weak answers copied sentences without explaining the effect on profit.
questions.fix: Show how revenue might rise and average costs fall, then argue the other side using the wage, union and emigration points.

questions.topic: Opportunity cost and a farmer's choice to grow apples
questions.issue: Fewer applied it to apples, and many simply said a choice had to be made.
questions.fix: Name an alternative crop, such as pears, and explain that cost, revenue and profit drive the choice.

questions.topic: Benefits of MNCs to their home countries
questions.issue: Generally poorly answered. Many gave host country benefits and mixed up remittances with profits.
questions.fix: The home country is where the MNC has its headquarters. Scheme points include profits sent home, lower prices from cheaper production abroad, and jobs at head office.

questions.topic: Determinants of price elasticity of demand
questions.issue: Poorly answered: some explained PED, gave supply factors such as time, or wrote vague wants and needs. Some correct answers were too long.
questions.fix: Just name two, such as substitutes, the proportion of income spent, or whether the good is a necessity or addictive.

questions.topic: Advantages to a firm of a horizontal merger
questions.issue: Many spent time describing the merger itself. A relatively common error was claiming a wider range of products.
questions.fix: Give two advantages, such as economies of scale lowering average costs and a larger market share from fewer rivals.

questions.topic: Why living standards differ between countries
questions.issue: Explanations were often weak. GDP was named without per head, and education without how it raises income.
questions.fix: Use GDP per head, and develop each factor, for example education raising skills and wages, so disposable income rises.
